nodes.name: Trunk-based development
nodes.description: A branching model where everyone merges small changes into one shared branch at least daily, keeping integration problems small.
nodes.markdown:
Trunk-based development is a branching model in which all developers merge small changes into one shared branch, called the trunk (usually `main`), at least once a day. Work happens directly on the trunk or on a [feature branch](node:Feature%20branch) that lives for a day or two. The trunk is kept in a state that could be released at any time.

The model addresses a familiar failure. Two developers work separately for three weeks, each with passing tests, then spend days resolving conflicts because both changed the same modules. Each branch worked alone, but the combination was never tested until the merge. Merging daily keeps each conflict small, and it makes [continuous integration](node:Continuous%20integration) possible because there is one line of code to integrate against.

| Aspect          | Long-lived branches           | Trunk-based development       |
| --------------- | ----------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Branch lifetime | Weeks or months               | Hours to a couple of days     |
| Merge size      | Large                         | Small                         |
| Conflicts       | Found late, in bulk           | Found early, one at a time    |
| Unfinished work | Hidden on the branch          | Merged, but switched off      |

Unfinished work is merged behind a [feature flag](node:Feature%20flag), which keeps the code inactive in production. Another option is branch by abstraction, where a new implementation is built behind an existing interface and swapped in once ready. Database changes follow [expand and contract](node:Expand%20and%20contract) for the same reason: each small step must be safe to ship alone.

The model depends on supporting habits. A fast automated [pipeline](node:Pipeline) must run on every change, reviews must happen within hours, and a broken trunk must be fixed or reverted before other work lands. Without those habits, frequent merges spread breakage to everyone.
quotes: My branch is three weeks old and the rebase has forty conflicts.
That's what trunk-based development avoids. Split it up, merge the refactor today, and put the new checkout behind a flag.

nodes.name: Feature branch
nodes.description: A Git branch that holds one change, such as a feature or bug fix, until it is reviewed and merged into the main branch.
nodes.markdown:
A feature branch is a Git branch created from the main branch to hold one change, such as a new endpoint or a bug fix, until it is reviewed and merged back. It lets a developer commit unfinished work without affecting anyone else, and it gives reviewers a single diff to read, usually through a pull request (a request to review and merge a branch).

| Step | Who        | What happens                                                        |
| ---- | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | Developer  | Creates the branch from the latest main                             |
| 2    | Developer  | Commits and pushes the change                                       |
| 3    | [CI](node:Continuous%20integration) | Builds and tests the branch                |
| 4    | Reviewer   | Reads the diff and requests changes or approves                     |
| 5    | Developer  | Updates from main and resolves any conflicts                        |
| 6    | Merge tool | Merges the change and deletes the branch                            |

The common problem is a branch that lives too long. Main moves on while the branch stands still, so the diff grows, reviewers put it off, and the final merge brings conflicts that are tedious and easy to get wrong.

A branch can also pass every check and still break main after merging, because the checks ran against an older copy of main. This is a semantic conflict: Git merges the text cleanly, but one side renamed a function the other side started calling.

Two practices reduce the risk. Keeping branches to a day or two, as in [trunk-based development](node:Trunk-based%20development), limits how far they can drift. A merge queue, which tests each pull request against the latest main plus the changes ahead of it before merging, catches semantic conflicts before they land. Large work can be split into small merges by hiding incomplete behaviour behind a [feature flag](node:Feature%20flag).
quotes: Both PRs were green, so why is main failing?
Your feature branch was tested before Sam's rename landed. Git merged them without a conflict, but your code still calls the old function. We should turn on the merge queue.

nodes.name: Continuous integration
nodes.description: The practice of merging work into a shared branch frequently, with an automated build and tests running on every change.
nodes.markdown:
Continuous integration (CI) is the practice of merging every developer's work into a shared branch frequently, with an automated build and test run on each change. The term describes a team habit as well as tooling. A team with a CI server whose branches stay unmerged for weeks has automated tests, but it is not integrating continuously.

CI addresses the "works on my machine" problem. A change passes on a laptop with a particular runtime version, a leftover environment variable, and a cached dependency, then fails for everyone else. A CI run starts from a clean checkout in a defined environment, so hidden assumptions show up as failures within minutes of the push.

A [pipeline](node:Pipeline) usually orders its checks so that fast ones fail first:

| Check             | What it catches                                    |
| ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| Lint and format   | Style problems and simple mistakes                 |
| Compile or build  | Syntax errors, type errors, missing imports        |
| Unit tests        | Broken logic in individual functions               |
| Integration tests | Components that fail when run together             |
| Packaging         | A [build artifact](node:Build%20artifact) that cannot be produced |

Three habits keep CI useful. First, a failing main branch is fixed or reverted before other work continues, because everyone branching from it inherits the failure. Second, the run stays fast enough that people wait for the result instead of switching tasks. Third, flaky tests, which pass or fail at random on the same code, are fixed or quarantined. When a suite is flaky, people learn to press "re-run" until it goes green, and real failures start being dismissed as noise.

CI stops at verifying the change. Getting the verified change to users is the job of [continuous delivery](node:Continuous%20delivery) or [continuous deployment](node:Continuous%20deployment).
quotes: CI failed on my PR but the test passes locally.
Check the Node version in the workflow. CI runs from a clean checkout, so it won't have whatever you installed globally.

nodes.name: Continuous delivery
nodes.description: Keeping every change that passes the pipeline ready to release, with a human deciding when it goes to production.
nodes.markdown:
Continuous delivery is the practice of keeping every change that passes the automated [pipeline](node:Pipeline) in a state that can be released to production at any time. The final production deployment is a human decision, usually a button press or an approved promotion. The abbreviation CD is ambiguous because it also stands for [continuous deployment](node:Continuous%20deployment), which removes that human step.

| Practice               | Build and test | Ready to release | Production deploy |
| ---------------------- | -------------- | ---------------- | ----------------- |
| [Continuous integration](node:Continuous%20integration) | Automatic | Not guaranteed | Separate process |
| Continuous delivery    | Automatic      | Always           | Manual decision   |
| Continuous deployment  | Automatic      | Always           | Automatic         |

The problem it addresses is the large, stressful release. When a team ships every few months, each release bundles many unrelated changes, needs a code freeze, and often runs late into the evening. If production breaks, nobody can tell which of the many commits caused it. Shipping small batches means each release contains little, so a failure is easier to trace and to reverse with a [rollback](node:Rollback).

Continuous delivery needs a few things in place. Each change produces one versioned [build artifact](node:Build%20artifact), and that same artifact moves through test, staging, and production. Deployment is scripted, so the production deployment uses the steps already exercised in staging. Configuration lives outside the artifact, so one build can run in every environment.

The manual gate is useful where release timing is a business or compliance decision: a launch tied to an announcement, a required sign-off, or a customer maintenance window. The gate should be a decision only. If pressing the button also requires a runbook of manual steps, the team does not yet have continuous delivery.
quotes: Can we ship the pricing fix this afternoon, or do we wait for the release train?
We have continuous delivery now. Build 412 already passed staging, so someone only needs to approve the production step.

nodes.name: Continuous deployment
nodes.description: Automatically releasing every change that passes the pipeline to production, with no human approval step.
nodes.markdown:
Continuous deployment is the practice of automatically releasing every change that passes the [pipeline](node:Pipeline) to production, with no human approval step. It extends [continuous delivery](node:Continuous%20delivery), where a person still chooses when to deploy. Under continuous deployment, merging to the main branch is the decision to ship.

Removing the human gate moves the responsibility for safety into automation. A bad change that the checks miss can reach users within minutes of being merged, so the safeguards have to exist before the gate is removed:

| Safeguard                | What it provides                                                     |
| ------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Reliable automated tests | Confidence that a green run means the change works                   |
| [Canary release](node:Canary%20release) | Exposes a small share of traffic to the change first  |
| Health-based promotion   | Stops the rollout when error rate or latency worsens                 |
| Automated [rollback](node:Rollback) | Returns to the previous version without waiting for a person |
| [Feature flag](node:Feature%20flag) | Ships code switched off and enables it separately        |

Feature flags matter here because they separate deploying from releasing. Code can reach production on every merge while the behaviour stays off until product, support, and documentation are ready. Without flags, every merged change becomes visible to users, and developers start holding back merges, which recreates long-lived branches.

Database changes need particular care. An automated deploy will run a schema change as readily as a code change, and a destructive migration cannot be undone by redeploying old code. Teams use [expand and contract](node:Expand%20and%20contract) so each deploy stays compatible with the version before it.

Continuous deployment does not suit every product. Mobile apps pass through store review, firmware is hard to update once shipped, and some regulated environments require a recorded human approval. Those teams usually stop at continuous delivery.
quotes: Who approved this going to production? I only merged it ten minutes ago.
Nobody has to. We use continuous deployment, so the merge was the approval. If the canary's error rate had climbed, it would have rolled itself back.

nodes.name: Pipeline
nodes.description: An automated sequence of build, test, and release steps that runs when code changes, defined in a file stored with the code.
nodes.markdown:
A pipeline is an automated sequence of steps that takes a code change from commit to a tested, packaged, and possibly deployed result. Pipelines are usually defined in a file stored with the code. A runner, which is a machine that executes the work, starts one when an event occurs, such as a push or a merged pull request.

| Level   | Meaning                         | Example                  |
| ------- | ------------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| Trigger | The event that starts a run     | Push to `main`           |
| Stage   | An ordered group of jobs        | Test                     |
| Job     | A set of steps on one runner    | Unit tests on Node 22    |
| Step    | A single command or action      | `npm test`               |

A minimal definition in GitHub Actions syntax:

```yaml
on: [push]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
```

A typical pipeline supports [continuous integration](node:Continuous%20integration) in its early stages, then produces a [build artifact](node:Build%20artifact), publishes it to an [artifact registry](node:Artifact%20registry), and deploys it through environments.

Slow pipelines are a common complaint. When a run takes forty minutes, developers batch up changes, stop watching results, and lose context before a failure comes back. The usual fixes are to run cheap checks first so failures appear early, cache dependencies between runs, split tests across parallel jobs, and run expensive suites only where they are relevant.

A job can pass locally and fail in the pipeline. Runners start from a clean environment, so anything that depended on a globally installed tool, a local file, or an unset environment variable breaks there. Treat that failure as information about a hidden dependency.

Pipelines often hold credentials that can publish packages or change production, which makes them an attack target in the [software supply chain](node:Software%20supply%20chain). Limit each job's permissions, and do not expose secrets to runs triggered by untrusted pull requests.
quotes: The pipeline's been stuck on integration tests for half an hour again.
Move lint and unit tests ahead of them so bad commits fail in two minutes, then split the integration suite across four jobs.

nodes.name: Build artifact
nodes.description: The packaged output of a build, such as a binary, archive, or container image, that is versioned and deployed.
nodes.markdown:
A build artifact is the packaged output of a build: the file or bundle that actually gets deployed. Depending on the stack, it might be a compiled binary, a Java JAR, a zip of bundled JavaScript, a Python wheel, or a [container image](node:Container%20image). The artifact is produced once by the [pipeline](node:Pipeline), given a version, and stored in an [artifact registry](node:Artifact%20registry).

The rule that follows is "build once, deploy many". The same artifact moves from test to staging to production, and only its configuration changes between environments. If each environment builds from source separately, the builds can differ. A dependency range may resolve to a newer release, a base image may have changed, or the compiler on one runner may differ. This produces a confusing failure: staging passed, production is broken, and the source commit is identical in both.

| Approach                 | What staging tested        | What production runs       |
| ------------------------ | -------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| Rebuild per environment  | Build A from commit `abc`  | Build B from commit `abc`  |
| Promote one artifact     | Build A from commit `abc`  | Build A from commit `abc`  |

Keeping one artifact across environments has consequences for how it is built. Environment-specific values such as database URLs must be supplied at runtime through environment variables or mounted files. Credentials must not be baked in, because anyone who can download the artifact could read them.

An artifact should be traceable. Record the commit it came from, its version, and a checksum or digest (a hash of its contents) so you can prove that what is running is what was tested. An [SBOM](node:SBOM) can be published alongside it to list what it contains. Keep previous artifacts available, because a fast [rollback](node:Rollback) depends on redeploying an earlier one instead of rebuilding it under pressure.
quotes: Staging is fine but prod throws an import error on the same commit.
Are we rebuilding for each environment? Promote the build artifact that passed staging instead, so a dependency can't shift between the two.

nodes.name: Artifact registry
nodes.description: A versioned store for build outputs and packages that pipelines publish to and deployments pull from.
nodes.markdown:
An artifact registry is a server that stores versioned build outputs and packages, so that [pipelines](node:Pipeline) can publish to it and deployments can pull from it. It may hold npm packages, Maven JARs, Python wheels, [Helm](node:Helm) charts, and [container images](node:Container%20image). JFrog Artifactory, Sonatype Nexus, and GitHub Packages are examples. A [container registry](node:Container%20registry) is the same idea specialised for images.

Registries commonly serve three kinds of repository:

| Type    | Contains                                      | Used for                                   |
| ------- | --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Hosted  | Your own [build artifacts](node:Build%20artifact) | Publishing internal packages and releases |
| Proxy   | Cached copies from a public registry          | Faster builds, tolerance of upstream outages |
| Virtual | One URL combining hosted and proxy            | Simple client configuration                |

A proxy repository addresses a failure many teams meet once. The public package registry has an outage, or a maintainer removes a package, and every build fails even though nobody changed any code. With a proxy in front, versions fetched earlier are still served from the cache.

A proxy also needs careful configuration. If a build looks up an internal package name and the registry also checks public sources, an attacker can publish a package with the same name and a higher version number. This is called dependency confusion, and it is a [software supply chain](node:Software%20supply%20chain) risk. Scope internal names so that they resolve only to the hosted repository.

Published versions should be immutable. If `2.3.1` can be overwritten, two deployments of the same version can contain different code, and any recorded checksum stops matching. Retention rules need similar thought. Storage grows quickly, so old versions get cleaned up, but a policy that deletes by age can remove the version you need for a [rollback](node:Rollback). Exclude anything currently deployed or recently released.
quotes: The rollback failed with a 404 on the old package.
The artifact registry's cleanup job deleted everything older than 30 days. Change the policy to keep the last ten releases regardless of age.

nodes.name: Semantic versioning
nodes.description: A MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH version format where each number signals whether a release breaks, extends, or fixes the public API.
nodes.markdown:
Semantic versioning (SemVer) is a version number format, `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, where each part tells consumers what kind of change a release contains. It applies to a declared public API, meaning whatever other code is expected to depend on.

| Part  | Example           | Increment when                          | Safe to adopt automatically? |
| ----- | ----------------- | --------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| MAJOR | `1.4.2` → `2.0.0` | A change breaks existing consumers      | No, read the release notes   |
| MINOR | `1.4.2` → `1.5.0` | Functionality is added compatibly       | Usually                      |
| PATCH | `1.4.2` → `1.4.3` | A bug is fixed compatibly               | Usually                      |

Incrementing a number resets those to its right. Two suffixes extend the format. A pre-release such as `2.0.0-rc.1` sorts before `2.0.0`. Build metadata such as `2.0.0+abc123` is ignored when comparing versions.

Version ranges in package managers rely on these promises. In npm, `^1.4.2` accepts anything below `2.0.0`, and `~1.4.2` accepts anything below `1.5.0`. Versions below `1.0.0` are treated differently, because the specification says anything may change during initial development. For that reason `^0.4.2` only accepts `0.4.x`.

SemVer is a statement of intent by the maintainer, and no tool enforces it. A library can publish a "patch" that changes behaviour you relied on, and your build breaks on a Monday morning with no change in your own code. Sometimes the maintainer considers the old behaviour a bug, while you considered it a feature. This is the reason to commit a lockfile and use [dependency pinning](node:Dependency%20pinning), so that upgrades happen deliberately and go through [continuous integration](node:Continuous%20integration).

Applications that have no consumers of their API get less value from SemVer. A deployed web service is often better identified by a commit hash or build number, and SemVer is kept for libraries, APIs, and [Helm](node:Helm) charts.
quotes: It's only a patch bump, so I merged it without testing.
Semantic versioning is a promise, not a guarantee. That patch changed the date parser and broke invoices, so let the upgrade run through CI first.

nodes.name: Feature flag
nodes.description: A runtime switch that turns code paths on or off without a deploy, separating shipping code from releasing behaviour.
nodes.markdown:
A feature flag is a runtime switch that turns a code path on or off without a new deployment. The code ships to production inside a conditional, and a configuration value or flag service decides who gets which path. This separates deploying code from releasing behaviour.

```ts
if (flags.isEnabled("new-checkout", { userId })) {
  return renderNewCheckout();
}
return renderOldCheckout();
```

Flags come in several kinds, with different lifespans:

| Type         | Purpose                                     | Expected lifespan |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------- | ----------------- |
| Release      | Hide unfinished or unreleased work          | Days to weeks     |
| Experiment   | Compare variants in an A/B test             | Weeks             |
| Operational  | Kill switch to disable a costly feature     | Long-term         |
| Permission   | Enable features for a plan or customer      | Long-term         |

Release flags make [trunk-based development](node:Trunk-based%20development) practical, because incomplete work can merge while switched off. They also allow a gradual rollout by user percentage, and turning a flag off is usually much faster than a [rollback](node:Rollback) because nothing is rebuilt or redeployed. A [dark launch](node:Dark%20launch) often relies on one.

The cost is accumulated flags. Each boolean doubles the possible code paths in principle, and nobody tests every combination. A common incident is a flag that has been "on" for two years: someone removes it from the flag service, the default evaluates to false, and production falls back to an old code path that no longer works. Give each release flag an owner and a removal date, and delete the conditional once the rollout is complete.

Decide what happens when the flag service is unreachable. Clients should cache the last known values and define a safe default for each flag, so that an outage in the flag service does not change application behaviour.
quotes: The new search is causing timeouts. Do we need to roll back?
No, it's behind a feature flag. Turn it off for everyone now, and we can look at the query tomorrow.

nodes.name: Container
nodes.description: A process isolated by Linux kernel features, with its own filesystem and limits, sharing the host's kernel.
nodes.markdown:
A container is a running process, or group of processes, that the Linux kernel isolates from the rest of the machine. It gets its own filesystem from a [container image](node:Container%20image), its own view of the system through [Linux namespaces](node:Linux%20namespace), and resource limits through [cgroups](node:cgroup). It shares the host's kernel, which is the main difference from a virtual machine.

| Aspect    | Container                     | Virtual machine                       |
| --------- | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| Kernel    | Shares the host's kernel      | Runs its own kernel                   |
| Boundary  | Kernel isolation features     | Hypervisor (software that runs VMs)   |
| Startup   | Starts a process              | Boots an operating system             |
| Footprint | Application and its libraries | Full operating system                 |

Sharing a kernel has practical effects. A Linux container needs a Linux kernel, so Docker Desktop on macOS and Windows runs one inside a lightweight virtual machine. A kernel vulnerability can affect every container on the host, so the isolation is weaker than a VM's. CPU architecture also still matters: an image built only for ARM fails on an x86 host with `exec format error` unless emulation is available.

A container lives only as long as its main process. When that process exits, the container stops, even if other processes were running inside it. If a script starts a background daemon and then finishes, the container exits immediately.

Containers are disposable, and their writable filesystem is deleted along with them. A common early mistake is writing uploads or a database file to the container's local disk, then finding the data gone after the next deploy replaced it. Data that must survive belongs in a mounted volume or an external service. Treating containers as replaceable is what makes [immutable infrastructure](node:Immutable%20infrastructure) and [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes) scheduling workable.
quotes: All the uploaded avatars disappeared after this morning's deploy.
They were saved inside the container, so they went away when it was replaced. Put them in object storage or a mounted volume.

nodes.name: Container image
nodes.description: A read-only package of filesystem layers and startup metadata from which containers are created.
nodes.markdown:
A [container](node:Container) image is a read-only package containing everything needed to start one: a filesystem made of [image layers](node:Image%20layer), plus metadata such as the default command, environment variables, working directory, and user. An image is to a container roughly what a program file is to a running process. One image can start many identical containers.

Images are usually built from a [Dockerfile](node:Dockerfile) and follow the OCI (Open Container Initiative) format, so an image built with one tool can run on other compatible runtimes. They are stored in a [container registry](node:Container%20registry) and are a common form of [build artifact](node:Build%20artifact).

An image can be referred to in two ways:

| Reference | Example                 | Can it change?                       |
| --------- | ----------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Tag       | `api:1.4.2`, `api:latest` | Yes, a tag can be moved to a new image |
| Digest    | `api@sha256:9f86d0...`  | No, it is a hash of the content      |

The difference causes a recognisable failure. Two servers both run `api:latest`, but they behave differently because each pulled the tag at a different time and got a different image. The name `latest` has no special meaning. It is only the default tag used when none is specified, and it does not guarantee the newest build. In production, use a unique version tag per build, or a digest when you need an exact guarantee, as described in [dependency pinning](node:Dependency%20pinning).

One image name can cover several CPU architectures through a multi-platform index, a list pointing to one image per platform. If no entry matches the machine, the pull fails with a "no matching manifest" error.

Images accumulate known vulnerabilities over time as new flaws are disclosed. Rebuild them regularly on an updated base and use [image scanning](node:Image%20scanning) to find what needs attention.
quotes: Two nodes are running the same image but only one has the bug.
Same tag, or same digest? If we deployed `latest`, they may have pulled different builds. Compare the digests.

nodes.name: Dockerfile
nodes.description: A text file of ordered instructions that a builder executes to produce a container image.
nodes.markdown:
A Dockerfile is a text file of ordered instructions that a builder executes to produce a [container image](node:Container%20image). Each instruction starts from the result of the previous one, and those that change files produce a new [image layer](node:Image%20layer).

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .
USER node
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

| Instruction  | Runs at    | Purpose                                     |
| ------------ | ---------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| `FROM`       | Build      | Selects the base image                      |
| `COPY`       | Build      | Adds files from the build context           |
| `RUN`        | Build      | Executes a command and saves the result     |
| `ENV`        | Both       | Sets environment variables                  |
| `USER`       | Both       | Sets the user for later steps and at runtime |
| `ENTRYPOINT` | Start      | Sets the executable for the [container](node:Container) |
| `CMD`        | Start      | Sets default arguments or a default command |

Instruction order controls build speed. Builders reuse cached layers until they reach a step whose input changed, then rerun everything after it. If `COPY . .` comes before the dependency install, editing one source file reinstalls every package, and a build that should take seconds takes minutes. Copying the lockfile first, as above, keeps the install step cached until dependencies change.

Three other mistakes are common. Without a `.dockerignore` file, the build context can include `node_modules`, `.git`, and local `.env` files, and `COPY . .` puts them in the image. Passing a password through `ARG` or `ENV` can leave it readable in the image's metadata or history, so use the builder's secret mount feature. Containers run as root unless the image or runtime sets another user.

The form of `CMD` affects shutdown. `CMD node server.js` runs under a shell, which may not forward the stop signal to Node, so the container hangs until it is force-killed. The JSON form runs the process directly. To keep build tools out of the result, use a [multi-stage build](node:Multi-stage%20build).
quotes: Every [CI](node:Continuous%20integration) build reinstalls all our dependencies, even for a typo fix.
Your Dockerfile copies the whole repo before `npm ci`. Copy the lockfile first so the install layer stays cached.

nodes.name: Image layer
nodes.description: A read-only set of filesystem changes. Stacked layers form a container image and are cached and shared between images.
nodes.markdown:
An image layer is a read-only set of filesystem changes: files added, modified, or deleted relative to the layer below it. A [container image](node:Container%20image) is an ordered stack of these layers, and a union filesystem merges them into the single directory tree that a [container](node:Container) sees. In a [Dockerfile](node:Dockerfile), instructions such as `RUN`, `COPY`, and `ADD` each create a layer.

Layers are identified by a hash of their content, which gives three benefits:

| Benefit       | What happens                                                         |
| ------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Build caching | Unchanged steps reuse an existing layer                              |
| Faster pushes | A [container registry](node:Container%20registry) receives only the layers it lacks |
| Shared storage | Images with the same base keep one copy on disk                     |

When a container starts, the runtime adds a thin writable layer on top. Changing an existing file copies it into that layer first (copy-on-write), and the layer is deleted with the container.

Because lower layers are read-only, deleting a file in a later layer does not remove it. The later layer records a "whiteout" marker that hides the file, while the bytes remain in the earlier layer. For example, a Dockerfile downloads a 500 MB archive in one `RUN`, deletes it in the next, and the image stays 500 MB larger.

The same mechanism creates a security problem. If a credential was copied in and removed later, anyone who can pull the image can extract the earlier layer and read it. Treat any secret that ever entered a layer as leaked, and rotate it.

To keep layers small, create and delete temporary files within the same `RUN` command, or use a [multi-stage build](node:Multi-stage%20build). `docker history` shows what each layer added.
quotes: I added `rm -rf /tmp/build` at the end, but the image didn't shrink.
That's a new image layer hiding the files. The bytes are still in the earlier one. Do the cleanup in the same `RUN` step.

nodes.name: Multi-stage build
nodes.description: A Dockerfile with several FROM stages, where only selected outputs are copied into a smaller final image.
nodes.markdown:
A multi-stage build is a [Dockerfile](node:Dockerfile) with more than one `FROM` instruction, where each `FROM` starts a separate stage and later stages copy only the files they need from earlier ones. Compilers, package managers, and source code stay in the build stage. The final [container image](node:Container%20image) contains the application and its runtime needs.

```dockerfile
FROM golang:1.23 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /app ./cmd/api

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12
COPY --from=build /app /app
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]
```

Without this technique, a small service can ship as an image of more than a gigabyte because it includes the entire toolchain used to compile it. Large images are slower to push and pull, which slows deployments and the start of new replicas during scaling. Every extra package also adds findings to [image scanning](node:Image%20scanning) and gives an attacker more tools to use after a break-in.

| Final base    | Contains                             | Trade-off                                |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------- |
| Full distro   | Package manager, shell, utilities    | Large, easy to debug                     |
| Slim          | Reduced distribution                 | Smaller, still has a shell               |
| Distroless    | Runtime libraries, no shell          | Small, harder to debug                   |
| `scratch`     | Nothing                              | Needs a fully static binary              |

Smaller bases can fail in less obvious ways. A dynamically linked binary copied into `scratch` fails with `no such file or directory`, even though the file is there, because the missing item is the system's dynamic linker. Binaries built against glibc can fail the same way on Alpine, which uses musl. Apps that make HTTPS calls may also need CA certificates copied in, or every TLS connection fails. Build statically, or choose a base that matches the build stage.

A build can stop at a named stage using `--target`, which is useful for running tests in the build environment. Layers from earlier stages are not part of the final image, although they can remain in the builder's cache.
quotes: Why is a 20 MB Go service shipping as a 1.2 GB image?
It still has the whole Go toolchain in it. Switch to a multi-stage build and copy only the binary into a distroless base.

nodes.name: Linux namespace
nodes.description: A Linux kernel feature that gives a process its own isolated view of a resource such as process IDs, network, or mounts.
nodes.markdown:
A Linux namespace is a kernel feature that gives a group of processes their own isolated view of one system resource. A [container](node:Container) is largely an ordinary process placed in a set of these namespaces, with [cgroups](node:cgroup) limiting what it can consume.

| Namespace | Isolates                         | Effect inside a container                    |
| --------- | -------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| PID       | Process IDs                      | Main process appears as PID 1                |
| Network   | Interfaces, IPs, ports, routes   | Has its own `localhost`                      |
| Mount     | Filesystem mount points          | Sees the [image](node:Container%20image) as its root filesystem |
| UTS       | Hostname                         | Has its own hostname                         |
| IPC       | Shared memory, message queues    | Cannot reach other containers' queues        |
| User      | User and group IDs               | Root inside can map to non-root outside      |
| Cgroup    | View of the cgroup hierarchy     | Sees its own cgroup as the root              |
| Time      | Boot and monotonic clocks        | Can have offset clocks                       |

The network namespace explains a frequent beginner failure. An app in one container connects to a database at `localhost:5432` and gets "connection refused", although the database is running. `localhost` refers to the container's own namespace, where nothing listens on that port. Connect using the other container's service name instead. Inside a [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes) [Pod](node:Pod), the reverse applies: containers share one network namespace, so they do reach each other on `localhost`.

The PID namespace explains slow shutdowns. The kernel treats PID 1 specially: a signal with no installed handler is ignored instead of taking its default action. An app that never registers a `SIGTERM` handler therefore keeps running when asked to stop, and the runtime force-kills it after a timeout. Add a handler, or run a small init process such as `tini` as PID 1.

Namespaces hide resources but do not make a process secure by themselves. All containers on a host still share one kernel.
quotes: The API can't reach Redis on localhost, but Redis is definitely up.
Different containers, different network namespaces. `localhost` is the API container itself. Use the `redis` hostname.

nodes.name: cgroup
nodes.description: A Linux kernel feature that limits and measures the CPU, memory, I/O, and process count used by a group of processes.
nodes.markdown:
A cgroup (control group) is a Linux kernel feature that limits and measures the resources used by a group of processes. Where a [Linux namespace](node:Linux%20namespace) controls what a process can see, a cgroup controls how much it can use. [Container](node:Container) runtimes create a cgroup for each one, and the [resource requests and limits](node:Resource%20requests%20and%20limits) set in [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes) are enforced through them. Most current Linux distributions default to cgroup v2.

| Resource | Limit example                | What happens at the limit                     |
| -------- | ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| CPU      | 0.5 CPU                      | Processes are paused until the next period    |
| Memory   | 512 MiB                      | Reclaim is attempted, then the OOM killer runs |
| PIDs     | 200 processes                | Creating another process or thread fails      |
| Block I/O | Bytes or operations per second | Reads and writes are slowed                 |

The two limits behave very differently. Exceeding a memory limit gets a process killed, which appears in Kubernetes as [OOMKilled](node:OOMKilled). Exceeding a CPU limit only slows the process down, which makes it harder to notice.

CPU limits work as a quota per scheduling period, by default 100 ms. A limit of 0.5 CPU allows 50 ms of CPU time per period, counted across all threads. Four busy threads spend that in about 12.5 ms, then all of them are paused for the remaining 87.5 ms. The result is a service with latency spikes while its average CPU usage looks moderate. The metric to check is CPU throttling, reported in the cgroup's `cpu.stat` file.

Software inside the container may not know about these limits. Tools such as `free` read `/proc/meminfo`, which reports the host's memory. An application that sizes its heap or thread pool from host numbers can overrun its limit. Many language runtimes now read cgroup limits, but check yours.
quotes: P99 latency jumps every few seconds, but the CPU graph sits at 40%.
Check throttling. The cgroup quota could be used up early in each period, and the threads then sit paused until the next one.

nodes.name: Container registry
nodes.description: A server that stores container images and serves them to machines that need to run them.
nodes.markdown:
A [container](node:Container) registry is a server that stores [container images](node:Container%20image) and serves them to the machines that run them. A [pipeline](node:Pipeline) pushes a new image after a build, and a host or [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes) node pulls it before starting a container. Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry, Amazon ECR, and Harbor are examples. A general [artifact registry](node:Artifact%20registry) can often store images alongside other package types.

An image reference names its location in the registry:

| Part       | Example         | Meaning                                  |
| ---------- | --------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| Registry   | `ghcr.io`       | The server. Docker Hub if omitted        |
| Repository | `acme/api`      | A collection of related images           |
| Tag        | `1.4.2`         | A movable, human-readable label          |
| Digest     | `sha256:9f86...` | The immutable hash of the image manifest |

Together these form `ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2`. Pushes and pulls transfer only the [image layers](node:Image%20layer) the other side lacks, so images that share a base move quickly.

Registry problems usually appear in Kubernetes as `ErrImagePull`, followed by `ImagePullBackOff` while the kubelet (the agent on each node) waits between retries. The usual causes are a mistyped name, a tag that was never pushed, missing credentials for a private repository, or a rate limit. Docker Hub limits pulls, so a cluster that scales up can hit the limit and fail to start workloads that have nothing wrong with them. A pull-through cache, which is a local registry that fetches and stores upstream images on first use, avoids that dependency.

Two settings are worth enabling. Tag immutability, offered by many registries, prevents an existing tag from being pushed over, so `1.4.2` always means the same image. A retention policy removes old images to control storage costs, but it should keep anything currently deployed and enough history for a [rollback](node:Rollback). Registries can also run [image scanning](node:Image%20scanning) when an image is pushed.
quotes: The new [pods](node:Pod) are all stuck in ImagePullBackOff.
Check that the tag exists in the container registry. If it does, the node's pull secret has probably expired.

nodes.name: Kubernetes
nodes.description: A system that runs containers across a cluster of machines and continually works to match the state you declared.
nodes.markdown:
Kubernetes (often written K8s) is an open-source system that runs [containers](node:Container) across a group of machines, called a cluster. You describe the state you want, such as "three copies of this [image](node:Container%20image), reachable on this port", and Kubernetes starts, places, connects, and replaces workloads to keep that state true.

A cluster has two parts. The [control plane](node:Control%20plane) stores the desired state and makes decisions. Worker machines, called nodes, run the workloads inside [Pods](node:Pod).

Most work happens through a small set of object types:

| Need                          | Object                                                    |
| ----------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| Run a stateless app           | [Deployment](node:Kubernetes%20Deployment)                |
| Run an app with stable identity | [StatefulSet](node:StatefulSet)                         |
| Run one copy per node         | [DaemonSet](node:DaemonSet)                               |
| Give Pods a stable address    | [Service](node:Kubernetes%20Service)                      |
| Route outside HTTP traffic    | [Ingress](node:Ingress)                                   |
| Supply settings               | [ConfigMap](node:ConfigMap)                               |
| Supply credentials            | [Secret](node:Kubernetes%20Secret)                        |

The behaviour that defines Kubernetes is reconciliation. Controllers, which are background loops, compare the declared state with the actual state and act on any difference. For example, you delete a misbehaving Pod and a new one appears within seconds. You removed the instance but left the instruction that says it should exist. To stop it, scale down or delete the object that owns it.

Reconciliation also means that changes are asynchronous. A successful `kubectl apply` only records your intent in the API. It does not mean the app is running, so a deploy can "succeed" while every new Pod fails to start. Check the rollout status and Pod events afterwards.

Kubernetes adds real operational weight: networking, upgrades, access control, and many concepts to learn. A managed offering such as Amazon EKS, Google GKE, or Azure AKS runs the control plane for you, but your team still owns the workloads. A single small service often does not need it.
quotes: I keep deleting this broken pod and it keeps coming back.
That's Kubernetes doing its job. The Deployment still asks for three replicas, so scale that down or fix the image.

nodes.name: Control plane
nodes.description: The Kubernetes components that store cluster state, schedule workloads, and run the controllers that keep it as declared.
nodes.markdown:
The control plane is the set of [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes) components that stores cluster state and decides what should run where. Worker nodes run the applications. The control plane tells them what to run and tracks the result.

| Component                | Role                                                                 |
| ------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| API server               | Front door for all reads and writes, with authentication and validation |
| etcd                     | Consistent key-value store that holds all cluster state              |
| Scheduler                | Picks a node for each unscheduled [Pod](node:Pod)                    |
| Controller manager       | Runs the loops that reconcile actual state with desired state        |
| Cloud controller manager | Talks to the cloud provider for load balancers, routes, and nodes    |

Each worker node runs a kubelet, an agent that watches the API server and starts the Pod's [containers](node:Container) through a container runtime. Components communicate through the API server, and only the API server talks to etcd.

A typical sequence for creating a [Deployment](node:Kubernetes%20Deployment): the API server validates and stores it in etcd, a controller creates a [ReplicaSet](node:ReplicaSet) and Pods, the scheduler assigns each Pod to a node, and that node's kubelet starts it.

Control plane failure does not immediately stop applications. Containers on healthy nodes keep running and can keep serving traffic, while `kubectl` commands fail or time out. The damage is that nothing can change: no new deployments, no scaling, and no rescheduling of Pods from a node that dies.

etcd needs a majority of its members to accept writes, so production clusters run an odd number, usually three or five. Three members tolerate one failure, and five tolerate two. Losing etcd without a backup means losing the cluster's definition, so self-managed clusters need tested backups. Managed services such as EKS, GKE, and AKS operate the control plane for you.
quotes: kubectl is timing out. Is the site down?
No, the app's still serving. The control plane is having trouble, so running pods are fine, but hold off on deploys until it recovers.

nodes.name: Pod
nodes.description: The smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes, made of one or more containers that share a network identity and can share storage.
nodes.markdown:
A Pod is the smallest unit [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes) can deploy: one or more [containers](node:Container) scheduled together on the same node. Containers in a Pod share a network namespace, so they have one IP address and reach each other on `localhost`, and they can mount the same volumes. Most Pods hold one application container, sometimes with a sidecar that ships logs or an init container that runs setup before the app starts.

Pods are disposable. A Pod is bound to one node and is not moved. If the node fails, or the Pod is deleted, a controller such as a [Deployment](node:Kubernetes%20Deployment) creates a replacement with a new name and a new IP address. Code that stores a Pod IP in configuration breaks the next time that happens, so clients should connect through a [Service](node:Kubernetes%20Service).

A restart is different from a replacement. When a container crashes, the kubelet (the agent on each node) restarts that container inside the same Pod, which keeps its name and IP. Files in the container's writable layer are lost, while an `emptyDir` volume survives until the Pod is removed.

| Phase     | Meaning                                                        |
| --------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Pending   | Accepted, but not all containers have started yet              |
| Running   | Bound to a node, with at least one container running or starting |
| Succeeded | All containers exited successfully and will not restart        |
| Failed    | All containers stopped, and at least one failed                |
| Unknown   | The Pod's state cannot be obtained, often a node problem       |

A Pod stuck in Pending usually has no node that fits its [resource requests](node:Resource%20requests%20and%20limits), or it is waiting on a volume. The Events section of `kubectl describe pod` gives the reason. Statuses such as [CrashLoopBackOff](node:CrashLoopBackOff) appear in `kubectl get pods` but are not phases.
quotes: The payment service had the worker's IP hardcoded, and it broke after the node drain.
Pod IPs change whenever a pod gets replaced. Point it at the Service name instead.

nodes.name: Kubernetes Deployment
nodes.description: A Kubernetes object that runs a set of identical Pods and manages rolling updates and rollbacks through ReplicaSets.
nodes.markdown:
A [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes) Deployment is an object that declares how a stateless application should run: which [container image](node:Container%20image), how many replicas, and how to update them. It does not manage [Pods](node:Pod) directly. It creates a [ReplicaSet](node:ReplicaSet) for each version of the Pod template, and shifts replicas between them during an update.

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: api }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: api }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2
```

Changing anything in `template`, such as the image tag, triggers a [rolling deployment](node:Rolling%20deployment):

| Step | What happens                                                        |
| ---- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | A new ReplicaSet is created for the new template                    |
| 2    | It scales up, within the `maxSurge` allowance                       |
| 3    | Old Pods are removed as new ones pass their [readiness probe](node:Readiness%20probe), within `maxUnavailable` |
| 4    | The old ReplicaSet stays at zero replicas, available for [rollback](node:Rollback) |

Both `maxSurge` and `maxUnavailable` default to 25%. Changing only `replicas` scales the current ReplicaSet and does not start a rollout. Editing a [ConfigMap](node:ConfigMap) does not start one either, which is why a config change can appear to do nothing.

A failed rollout often looks like a hang. If new Pods never become ready, the update stops partway and old Pods keep serving, which protects users. After `progressDeadlineSeconds`, 600 by default, the Deployment reports `ProgressDeadlineExceeded`. It does not roll itself back. Someone must fix the image or run `kubectl rollout undo`. [Pipelines](node:Pipeline) should run `kubectl rollout status` so that a stuck rollout fails the job, because `kubectl apply` returns success as soon as the change is accepted.

Use a [StatefulSet](node:StatefulSet) instead when replicas need stable identities or individual storage.
quotes: [CI](node:Continuous%20integration) says the deploy passed, but we're still serving the old version.
Apply only submits the change. The Kubernetes Deployment is stuck because the new pods are failing readiness. Check `kubectl rollout status`.

nodes.name: ReplicaSet
nodes.description: A Kubernetes controller that keeps a set number of matching Pods running, usually created and managed by a Deployment.
nodes.markdown:
A ReplicaSet is a [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes) object that keeps a specified number of matching [Pods](node:Pod) running. If there are too few it creates more from its Pod template, and if there are too many it deletes the excess. It finds its Pods using a label selector, which is a query over key-value tags attached to objects.

You rarely create one by hand. A [Deployment](node:Kubernetes%20Deployment) creates and owns ReplicaSets, one per version of the Pod template. That is why Pod names have two generated parts: in `api-7d9f6c5b4-x2kqp`, `7d9f6c5b4` identifies the ReplicaSet and `x2kqp` identifies the Pod.

| Object     | Responsible for                              |
| ---------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| Deployment | Versions, rollout strategy, and history      |
| ReplicaSet | The replica count for one version            |
| Pod        | Running the [containers](node:Container)     |

During a [rolling deployment](node:Rolling%20deployment), the Deployment scales a new ReplicaSet up and the old one down. Old ReplicaSets stay at zero replicas so that a [rollback](node:Rollback) can scale one back up. `revisionHistoryLimit`, 10 by default, sets how many are kept. This is why `kubectl get rs` shows a list of entries with zero Pods, and they are normally safe to leave.

Three behaviours cause confusion. Manually scaling a ReplicaSet owned by a Deployment does not last, because the Deployment sets it back to the declared count. Editing the template of a standalone ReplicaSet does not update running Pods, because the template is only used when creating new ones, so the old [image](node:Container%20image) keeps running until those Pods are replaced. A ReplicaSet can also adopt existing Pods that have no owner and match its selector, so overlapping labels can cause it to take over or delete Pods you created separately.

To change the replica count or image, edit the Deployment.
quotes: I scaled the ReplicaSet to five, and it went straight back to three.
The Deployment owns it and still says three. Change the replica count on the Deployment.

nodes.name: Kubernetes Service
nodes.description: A Kubernetes object giving a changing set of Pods one stable virtual IP and DNS name, and spreading connections across them.
nodes.markdown:
A [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes) Service is an object that gives a changing set of [Pods](node:Pod) one stable address. Pods are replaced often and get new IPs each time, so clients connect to the Service's virtual IP or DNS name instead. A Service named `api` in namespace `shop` resolves at `api.shop.svc.cluster.local`, or `api` from within the same namespace.

A label selector chooses the Pods. Matching Pods are recorded in EndpointSlice objects, and kube-proxy, a component on each node, usually routes new connections to those passing their [readiness probe](node:Readiness%20probe).

| Type           | Reachable from                  | Typical use                                |
| -------------- | ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| `ClusterIP`    | Inside the cluster (default)    | Service-to-service traffic                 |
| `NodePort`     | A port on every node            | Simple external access, testing            |
| `LoadBalancer` | A cloud load balancer           | Exposing one service publicly              |
| `ExternalName` | DNS alias to an outside host    | Pointing at an external system             |

A "headless" Service, with `clusterIP: None`, has no virtual IP. DNS returns the individual Pod addresses, which a [StatefulSet](node:StatefulSet) uses to give each replica a stable name.

A frequent failure is a Service with no ready endpoints. Connections fail even though Pods are running, usually because the selector does not match the Pod labels or no Pod is ready. Check with `kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=api`. A wrong `targetPort` gives a similar symptom with endpoints present.

Balancing happens per connection, not per request. A client using one long-lived HTTP/2 or gRPC connection sends all its requests to one Pod, so one replica can be overloaded while others sit idle. Client-side balancing or a [service mesh](node:Service%20mesh) can spread those requests. For HTTP routing from outside the cluster, use [Ingress](node:Ingress).
quotes: The pods are healthy but the Service just times out.
Look at its endpoints. If the list is empty, the selector probably says `app: api` while the pods are labelled `app: api-server`.

nodes.name: Ingress
nodes.description: A Kubernetes object with HTTP routing rules that send outside traffic to Services, carried out by an ingress controller.
nodes.markdown:
An Ingress is a [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes) object that defines how HTTP and HTTPS traffic from outside the cluster reaches internal [Services](node:Kubernetes%20Service), based on hostname and URL path. One public entry point can route `app.example.com/api` to one Service and `app.example.com/` to another, and can terminate TLS (decrypt HTTPS) using a certificate stored in a [Kubernetes Secret](node:Kubernetes%20Secret).

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  ingressClassName: traefik
  rules:
    - host: app.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /api
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: api
                port: { number: 80 }
```

An Ingress object is only a set of rules, and Kubernetes itself does not act on them. An ingress controller, which is a reverse proxy running in the cluster such as Traefik or HAProxy, watches these objects and configures itself. This explains a common first experience: the Ingress is created without errors, its address stays blank, and nothing responds, because no controller is installed or `ingressClassName` does not match one.

Errors at this layer usually point to a specific cause:

| Symptom        | Likely cause                                                |
| -------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| 404            | No rule matches the host or path                            |
| 502            | Controller reached a backend that refused or dropped it     |
| 503            | The Service has no ready [Pods](node:Pod)                   |
| 504            | Backend too slow for the proxy's timeout                    |
| Wrong certificate | TLS host or Secret mismatch, or Secret in another namespace |

Exact responses vary by controller. Behaviour beyond basic routing, such as rewrites, rate limits, and timeouts, is usually set through controller-specific annotations, so an Ingress written for one controller may not work the same on another.

The Ingress API is frozen, and new features go to its successor, the Gateway API, which separates infrastructure and routing concerns into distinct objects. Ingress remains supported and widely used.
quotes: I created the Ingress, but the address column is empty and the domain doesn't resolve.
Is there a controller in this cluster? The object does nothing until something implements it, and your `ingressClassName` has to match.

nodes.name: ConfigMap
nodes.description: A Kubernetes object holding non-confidential settings that Pods read as environment variables or mounted files.
nodes.markdown:
A ConfigMap is a [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes) object that stores non-confidential configuration as key-value pairs, separately from the [container image](node:Container%20image). One image can then run in staging and production with different settings, which supports promoting a single [build artifact](node:Build%20artifact). A ConfigMap is limited to 1 MiB and must be in the same namespace as the [Pods](node:Pod) using it. Credentials belong in a [Kubernetes Secret](node:Kubernetes%20Secret) or external [secrets management](node:Secrets%20management).

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: api-config
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: info
  FEATURE_URL: https://flags.internal
```

The way a Pod consumes a ConfigMap decides what happens when it changes:

| Consumed as              | After the ConfigMap is edited                            |
| ------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| Environment variable     | No change until the [container](node:Container) restarts |
| Mounted volume           | Files update after a delay, and the app must re-read them |
| Volume with `subPath`    | No change until the container restarts                   |

The familiar symptom is editing a value, seeing the new value in `kubectl get configmap`, and finding that the application still behaves the old way. Editing a ConfigMap does not restart anything and does not trigger a [Kubernetes Deployment](node:Kubernetes%20Deployment) rollout. Run `kubectl rollout restart deployment/api`, or include a hash of the config as an annotation in the Pod template so that a config change produces a new rollout. [Helm](node:Helm) charts commonly do the second.

A shared, mutable ConfigMap also weakens [rollback](node:Rollback), because rolling back the Deployment does not restore old config values. Versioned names such as `api-config-v12`, referenced from the Pod template, tie configuration to the release.

A missing ConfigMap blocks startup. A missing environment reference shows `CreateContainerConfigError`, and a missing volume leaves the Pod in `ContainerCreating` with a mount error in its events.
quotes: I changed LOG_LEVEL to debug an hour ago and still see nothing.
It's injected as an env var from the ConfigMap, so running containers keep the old value. Do a rollout restart.

nodes.name: Kubernetes Secret
nodes.description: A Kubernetes object for small sensitive values. Its data is base64-encoded and is not encrypted by default.
nodes.markdown:
A [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes) Secret is an object for holding small pieces of sensitive data, such as passwords, API tokens, and TLS certificates, so they stay out of [container images](node:Container%20image) and [Pod](node:Pod) specs. Pods consume Secrets as environment variables or mounted files. The size limit is 1 MiB.

Secret values are base64-encoded, and base64 is a reversible text format that provides no protection. Anyone who can read the object can decode it with one command:

```sh
echo 'cGFzc3dvcmQ=' | base64 --decode
```

By default the API server also stores Secrets unencrypted in etcd, the cluster's database. A frequent mistake is committing a Secret manifest to Git because the values look scrambled. Rotate any value exposed this way.

Protecting Secrets takes several separate measures:

| Measure                | What it protects against                              |
| ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| Encryption at rest     | Someone reading etcd or its backups                   |
| RBAC (role-based access control) | Users and workloads reading Secrets via the API |
| Namespace separation   | Workloads in other namespaces mounting them           |
| External secret store  | Long-lived values living only in the cluster          |

Access rules have a gap that is easy to miss. Anyone allowed to create a Pod in a namespace can mount any Secret in that namespace and read it, even without permission to `get` Secrets directly. For stronger control, use dedicated [secrets management](node:Secrets%20management) and sync or inject values at runtime.

Encoding also causes a login failure. `echo "hunter2" | base64` includes a trailing newline, so the application sends a password ending in `\n` and authentication fails. Use `echo -n`, `kubectl create secret`, or the `stringData` field, which accepts plain text.

Updates behave like those of a [ConfigMap](node:ConfigMap): environment variables keep the old value until the [container](node:Container) restarts.
quotes: It's fine to commit this Secret YAML, the password is encoded.
That's base64, so anyone can decode it. Kubernetes doesn't encrypt it for you. Rotate that password and keep it in Vault.

nodes.name: StatefulSet
nodes.description: A Kubernetes workload giving each Pod a stable name, stable storage, and ordered rollout, for apps like databases.
nodes.markdown:
A StatefulSet is a [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes) workload object for applications whose replicas are not interchangeable, such as databases, message brokers, and consensus systems. Each [Pod](node:Pod) gets a stable ordinal name (`db-0`, `db-1`, `db-2`) and its own persistent volume. If `db-1` is replaced, the new Pod is also `db-1` and reattaches the same storage.

| Aspect       | [Deployment](node:Kubernetes%20Deployment) | StatefulSet                   |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------- |
| Pod names    | Random suffix                              | Stable ordinal                |
| Storage      | Usually shared or none                     | One volume claim per Pod      |
| Start order  | Parallel                                   | In order, 0 to N-1 by default |
| Update order | Surge and replace                          | Reverse order, N-1 to 0       |
| Network      | Shared [Service](node:Kubernetes%20Service) address | Per-Pod DNS name via a headless Service |

A headless Service (one with no virtual IP) gives each replica an address such as `db-0.db.prod.svc.cluster.local`, so peers and clients can reach a specific member. Storage is declared in `volumeClaimTemplates`, which create one PersistentVolumeClaim (a request for durable storage) per Pod.

A StatefulSet provides identity and ordering only. Replication, leader election, and failover belong to the software itself or to a [Kubernetes Operator](node:Kubernetes%20Operator).

Three behaviours often cause problems. Scaling down or deleting a StatefulSet leaves its volumes behind by default, and a later scale-up reattaches the old data. When a node becomes unreachable, its Pod is not recreated elsewhere, because two Pods with one identity could corrupt a shared volume. It stays stuck until the node returns or someone confirms the node is gone. With default ordering, a Pod that never becomes ready blocks the rollout, and it can stay blocked after the template is fixed until the broken Pod is deleted.
quotes: `db-2` has been Terminating for twenty minutes since that node died. Why isn't it rescheduled?
A StatefulSet won't start a second `db-2` until it knows the first is gone. Confirm the node is really dead before forcing it.

nodes.name: DaemonSet
nodes.description: A Kubernetes workload that runs one copy of a Pod on every eligible node, used for node-level agents.
nodes.markdown:
A DaemonSet is a [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes) workload object that runs one copy of a [Pod](node:Pod) on every eligible node. When a node joins the cluster it receives the Pod automatically, and when a node is removed its copy goes with it. There is no replica count to set, because the number of nodes determines the number of Pods.

DaemonSets suit software tied to the machine instead of to an application:

| Use                | Example job                                        |
| ------------------ | -------------------------------------------------- |
| Log collection     | Reads [container](node:Container) log files from the node's disk     |
| Metrics            | Reports node CPU, memory, and disk                 |
| Networking         | Runs the cluster network plugin or kube-proxy      |
| Storage            | Runs a node driver that mounts volumes             |
| Security           | Watches system calls or file changes on the host   |

Such Pods often use `hostPath` volumes, which mount a directory from the node, or host networking, so a compromised agent can affect the whole node. Grant only the access it needs.

The usual complaint is an agent missing from some nodes, which leaves gaps in logs or metrics from those machines. The cause is often a taint, a marker on a node that repels Pods unless they declare a matching toleration. Dedicated GPU nodes and [control plane](node:Control%20plane) nodes are commonly tainted. Compare `DESIRED` with the node count in `kubectl get daemonset`, then add the required toleration. A `nodeSelector` can also limit a DaemonSet deliberately to a subset of nodes.

A DaemonSet's cost multiplies by node count, because its [resource requests](node:Resource%20requests%20and%20limits) are reserved on every machine.

Updates use a rolling strategy by default, replacing one node's Pod at a time (`maxUnavailable: 1`). A bad version of a networking or storage agent can degrade every node it reaches, so watch the first few and run `kubectl rollout undo` at the first failure.
quotes: We have no logs from the GPU nodes.
Those nodes are tainted, so the logging DaemonSet never scheduled there. Add a toleration for the GPU taint.

nodes.name: Liveness probe
nodes.description: A periodic Kubernetes health check that restarts a container when it fails repeatedly.
nodes.markdown:
A liveness probe is a periodic health check, run by the kubelet (the agent on each node), that decides whether a [container](node:Container) should be restarted. When the probe fails `failureThreshold` times in a row, 3 by default, the kubelet kills the container and the [Pod](node:Pod)'s restart policy applies. The Pod stays on the same node and keeps its IP address.

```yaml
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /livez
    port: 8080
  periodSeconds: 10
  timeoutSeconds: 2
  failureThreshold: 3
```

A probe can be an HTTP request (a status from 200 to 399 passes), a TCP connection, a gRPC health check, or a command that must exit with 0.

Liveness probes exist for failures that a restart can fix, such as a deadlock where the process is still running but no longer doing work. Without one, [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes) only restarts a container when its process exits.

A badly designed probe can cause an outage. A frequent mistake is having the liveness endpoint check the database. When the database slows down, every replica fails its probe and restarts together, removing capacity and adding a burst of reconnections. A restart cannot fix a dependency, so the liveness check should only cover the process itself. Dependency checks belong in a [readiness probe](node:Readiness%20probe), which takes a Pod out of traffic without restarting it.

Timing causes the other common failure. An application that needs a minute to start gets killed before it finishes, restarts, and is killed again, which shows up as [CrashLoopBackOff](node:CrashLoopBackOff). Add a startup probe, which holds off liveness and readiness checks until it first succeeds. The default `timeoutSeconds` is 1, so a busy but healthy process can miss probes under load and be restarted.

To confirm the cause, look for `Liveness probe failed` in the events from `kubectl describe pod`.
quotes: Every pod restarted at once when Postgres had that slow spell.
Our liveness probe queries the database. Move that check to readiness, and have liveness confirm only that the process responds.

nodes.name: Readiness probe
nodes.description: A periodic Kubernetes check that removes a Pod from Service endpoints while it fails, without restarting it.
nodes.markdown:
A readiness probe is a periodic check, run by the kubelet (the agent on each node), that decides whether a [Pod](node:Pod) should receive traffic. While it fails, the Pod is marked not ready and removed from the endpoints of any [Service](node:Kubernetes%20Service) that selects it. The [container](node:Container) keeps running and is not restarted. When the probe passes again, the Pod returns to rotation.

[Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes) has three probe types, which answer different questions:

| Probe                                 | Question                  | On failure                        | Runs                  |
| ------------------------------------- | ------------------------- | --------------------------------- | --------------------- |
| Startup                               | Has it finished starting? | Container restarted at threshold  | Until first success   |
| [Liveness](node:Liveness%20probe)     | Is the process working?   | Container restarted               | After startup         |
| Readiness                             | Can it take traffic now?  | Removed from Service endpoints    | After startup, continuously |

Without a readiness probe, a Pod counts as ready once its containers start. Traffic then reaches an application that is still loading data or opening connections, and users see a burst of errors on every deploy.

Readiness also controls [rolling deployments](node:Rolling%20deployment). A [Deployment](node:Kubernetes%20Deployment) only continues replacing old Pods as new ones become ready, so a version that never passes stalls the rollout while the old version keeps serving. That protection disappears if the probe always returns success.

Shared dependencies need caution. If every replica's readiness depends on one cache and that cache goes down, all Pods leave the endpoints at once, and a partial degradation becomes a full outage. Consider serving reduced functionality instead.

Shutdown is a separate gap. When a Pod is deleted, endpoint removal and the `SIGTERM` signal happen at about the same time, so a few requests can still arrive after the process begins to exit. Keep serving briefly after `SIGTERM`, or add a short `preStop` delay.
quotes: We get a spike of 503s for about thirty seconds on every deploy.
The new pods take traffic before the cache warms up. Add a readiness probe that passes only once it's loaded.

nodes.name: Resource requests and limits
nodes.description: Per-container CPU and memory settings. Requests guide Pod placement, and limits cap what a container may use at runtime.
nodes.markdown:
Resource requests and limits are per-[container](node:Container) CPU and memory settings in [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes). A request is the amount the scheduler reserves when choosing a node. A limit is the ceiling enforced at runtime through [cgroups](node:cgroup). CPU is measured in cores or millicores (`500m` is half a CPU), and memory in bytes (`256Mi`).

```yaml
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 250m
    memory: 256Mi
  limits:
    memory: 512Mi
```

| Aspect             | Request                                     | Limit                       |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| Used by            | Scheduler, and the kernel for CPU shares    | Kernel at runtime           |
| Exceeding CPU      | Allowed when the node has spare CPU         | Throttled (paused)          |
| Exceeding memory   | Allowed, but raises eviction risk           | Container is [OOMKilled](node:OOMKilled) |

Scheduling uses requests, not actual usage. A [Pod](node:Pod) stays Pending with an `Insufficient cpu` or `Insufficient memory` event when no node has enough unreserved capacity, even if the machines are mostly idle. Requests set too low let the scheduler pack too many Pods on one node.

If only a limit is set, the request defaults to the same value. The settings also determine a Pod's quality of service class:

| Class      | Condition                                          |
| ---------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| Guaranteed | Every container has CPU and memory requests equal to limits |
| Burstable  | At least one request or limit, but not Guaranteed  |
| BestEffort | No requests or limits at all                       |

When a node runs short of memory, the kubelet evicts Pods, generally starting with those using more than their request. BestEffort Pods have no request, so they are exposed first.

A common starting point is to set memory requests from observed usage, with a limit at or slightly above that value. CPU limits can throttle a service while the node has idle CPU, so some teams set only a CPU request. The [Horizontal Pod Autoscaler](node:Horizontal%20Pod%20Autoscaler) calculates CPU utilisation against the request.
quotes: The pod's stuck in Pending, but the nodes are only at 20% CPU.
Scheduling looks at requests, not usage. Those nodes are fully reserved, and this pod is asking for four cores. Lower its resource requests.

nodes.name: OOMKilled
nodes.description: A Kubernetes status meaning the kernel killed a container for running out of memory, usually at its memory limit.
nodes.markdown:
OOMKilled is the status [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes) reports when the Linux kernel's out-of-memory (OOM) killer ends a [container](node:Container). It usually means the container reached the memory limit in its [resource requests and limits](node:Resource%20requests%20and%20limits), which is enforced by a [cgroup](node:cgroup). It can also happen when the whole node runs out of memory.

The kill uses `SIGKILL`, which a process cannot catch, so the application cannot log an error or shut down cleanly. The typical symptom is a service that restarts at random with logs that stop without explanation. The evidence is in the [Pod](node:Pod) status:

```text
Last State:  Terminated
  Reason:    OOMKilled
  Exit Code: 137
```

Exit code 137 means 128 plus signal 9 (`SIGKILL`). It does not prove an OOM kill on its own, because any `SIGKILL` produces it, including one sent when a process ignores a shutdown request. Check for the `OOMKilled` reason as well. Repeated kills usually lead to [CrashLoopBackOff](node:CrashLoopBackOff).
