| Memory graph before the kill | Likely cause                  | What to do                              |
| ---------------------------- | ----------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Climbs steadily over hours   | Memory leak                   | Take a heap profile and fix the leak    |
| Sudden spike                 | Large request, file, or batch | Stream data or bound the work size      |
| Flat, close to the limit     | Limit too low                 | Raise it based on observed usage        |
| Container low, node full     | Node memory pressure          | Fix requests, or add node capacity      |

A heap setting such as the JVM's `-Xmx` or Node's `--max-old-space-size` covers only part of a process's memory. Thread stacks, native buffers, and non-reclaimable page cache also count toward the limit, so leave headroom.

Raising the limit is the right fix only when usage is legitimately higher. With a leak, it just delays the next kill.
quotes: The worker dies every few hours and the logs just stop.
Check the last state. If it's OOMKilled with exit code 137, the kernel killed it, so it never had a chance to log anything.

nodes.name: CrashLoopBackOff
nodes.description: A Kubernetes status meaning a container keeps exiting and the kubelet is waiting longer between each restart attempt.
nodes.markdown:
CrashLoopBackOff is a [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes) status meaning a [container](node:Container) keeps exiting and the kubelet (the agent on each node) is waiting before restarting it again. It describes the restart pattern. The cause is whatever made the process exit.

The wait doubles after each failed restart: 10 seconds, 20, 40, and so on, capped at five minutes. The timer resets once a container has run for 10 minutes without a problem. This is why a [Pod](node:Pod) can look as though nothing is happening for several minutes, then briefly show Running, then return to CrashLoopBackOff.

The first diagnostic steps are:

```sh
kubectl logs my-pod --previous
kubectl describe pod my-pod
```

The `--previous` flag matters because the current container may have just started and logged nothing, while the crashed instance holds the error. `describe` shows the last exit code and recent events.

| Exit code | Meaning                 | Usual cause                                                  |
| --------- | ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| 0         | Process finished        | A one-off script run as a long-lived service                 |
| 1         | Application error       | Bad config, missing env var, failed connection at startup    |
| 126       | Cannot execute          | A script without execute permission                          |
| 127       | Command not found       | A shell entrypoint calling a missing program                 |
| 137       | `SIGKILL`               | [OOMKilled](node:OOMKilled), or a forced stop after a failed probe |
| 143       | `SIGTERM`               | Asked to stop, often by a failed [liveness probe](node:Liveness%20probe) |

Exit code 0 can also produce this status. A [Deployment](node:Kubernetes%20Deployment) requires `restartPolicy: Always`, so a container that completes successfully is restarted. Use a Job (a workload that runs to completion) for one-off tasks.

If logs are empty, the runtime may have failed to start the command, which `describe` reports as a start error. Check the entrypoint and [image](node:Container%20image) architecture, or debug with an ephemeral container through `kubectl debug`.

Restarting or deleting the Pod rarely helps, since the replacement hits the same failure.
quotes: The new release is in CrashLoopBackOff and the logs are empty.
Run logs with `--previous`, you're looking at the fresh container. And check the exit code in describe.

nodes.name: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
nodes.description: A Kubernetes controller that changes a workload's replica count based on CPU, memory, or custom metrics.
nodes.markdown:
A Horizontal [Pod](node:Pod) Autoscaler (HPA) is a [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes) controller that adjusts the number of Pod replicas in a workload, such as a [Deployment](node:Kubernetes%20Deployment), according to observed metrics. "Horizontal" means adding or removing replicas, as opposed to giving each one more CPU or memory. By default it re-evaluates every 15 seconds using this calculation:

```text
desired = ceil(current replicas × current metric / target metric)
```

With 4 replicas averaging 90% CPU against a 60% target, the result is `ceil(4 × 90 / 60) = 6`. The controller skips changes when the ratio of current to target is within 10% of 1.0, which prevents constant small adjustments.

```yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: api }
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 20
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 60 }
```

CPU utilisation is calculated against the Pod's CPU request from its [resource requests and limits](node:Resource%20requests%20and%20limits). If `kubectl get hpa` shows `<unknown>` as the current value and nothing scales, the usual cause is a missing CPU request or a missing metrics-server (the add-on that reports resource usage).

Other common problems:

| Symptom                              | Cause                                         | Fix                                    |
| ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| Replicas reset on each deploy        | Manifest also sets `spec.replicas`            | Remove `replicas` from the manifest    |
| Slow to scale down                   | Default five-minute stabilisation window      | Tune `behavior` if needed              |
| New Pods stay Pending                | Cluster has no spare node capacity            | Add a node autoscaler                  |
| No scaling during overload           | Bottleneck is I/O, so CPU stays low           | Scale on queue depth or request rate   |

The HPA reacts after load has already risen, and new Pods still need time to pull [images](node:Container%20image) and pass their [readiness probe](node:Readiness%20probe). For sharp spikes, keep `minReplicas` high enough to absorb the first wave.
quotes: Traffic tripled and the HPA didn't add a single pod.
Its target says `<unknown>`. The [container](node:Container) has no CPU request, so it has nothing to compute utilisation against.

nodes.name: Helm
nodes.description: A package manager for Kubernetes that renders templated manifests from values and tracks each install as a release.
nodes.markdown:
Helm is a package manager for [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes). It bundles the manifests an application needs into a versioned package called a chart, fills in templates using configuration values, applies the result to a cluster, and records each install or upgrade so it can be reversed.

| Term       | Meaning                                                     |
| ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| Chart      | A package of templates, defaults, and metadata              |
| Values     | Configuration supplied to the templates                     |
| Template   | A manifest with placeholders, written in Go template syntax |
| Release    | One installed instance of a chart in a cluster              |
| Revision   | A numbered version of a release                             |
| Repository | A place that hosts charts, often an OCI [container registry](node:Container%20registry) |

A template fragment looks like this:

```yaml
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
```

The same chart can then deploy to staging and production with a different values file. Charts carry a [semantic version](node:Semantic%20versioning), so a team can install third-party software at a known version.

Generating YAML through text templates has known failure modes. Wrong indentation produces invalid manifests, or valid ones with a field in the wrong place. A misspelled key in a values file is usually ignored without any warning, so an override appears to do nothing. Run `helm template` or `helm upgrade --dry-run` to inspect the rendered output before applying it.

A successful `helm upgrade` can also mislead. Without a wait option, Helm reports success once the API server accepts the resources, while the new [Pods](node:Pod) may be crashing. Use `--wait` with a timeout in [pipelines](node:Pipeline), and `--rollback-on-failure` to undo a failed upgrade. Helm 3 calls this flag `--atomic`, and Helm 4 renamed it.

`helm rollback` restores an earlier revision's manifests by creating a new revision. It does not undo data changes. Helm stores release history in [Secrets](node:Kubernetes%20Secret) in the release's namespace by default, so deleting those Secrets makes Helm lose track of the release.
quotes: I set `replicas: 5` in the values file, and it's still running two.
The chart reads `replicaCount`, so Helm ignored your key. Run `helm template` and check the output.

nodes.name: Kubernetes Operator
nodes.description: A custom Kubernetes controller that automates operating an application, driven by custom resource types.
nodes.markdown:
A [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes) Operator is a custom controller that automates the operation of a specific application by extending the Kubernetes API. It encodes tasks a human administrator would otherwise perform, such as setting up replication, taking backups, handling failover, and running version upgrades.

An Operator has three parts:

| Part                               | Role                                                  |
| ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| CustomResourceDefinition (CRD)     | Adds a new object type to the Kubernetes API          |
| Custom resource                    | An instance of that type, stating what you want       |
| Controller                         | Watches those objects and acts to make them true      |

With a PostgreSQL Operator such as CloudNativePG, a database cluster becomes one short manifest:

```yaml
apiVersion: postgresql.cnpg.io/v1
kind: Cluster
metadata:
  name: orders-db
spec:
  instances: 3
  storage:
    size: 20Gi
```

The controller creates the [Pods](node:Pod), storage, and [Services](node:Kubernetes%20Service), configures replication, and promotes a replica if the primary fails. It runs a reconcile loop, the same pattern built-in controllers use: read the desired state, inspect the actual state, and act on the difference.

Operators are useful for stateful software, where a [StatefulSet](node:StatefulSet) supplies identity and storage but knows nothing about the application's failover process. For a stateless app, a [Deployment](node:Kubernetes%20Deployment) or [Helm](node:Helm) chart is usually enough.

An Operator is extra software you must run and trust. It often holds broad cluster permissions, its CRDs need upgrading alongside it, and a bug in it acts automatically on production systems. If it stops running, nothing reconciles, so failover and repair stop too.

A recognisable failure comes from removing an Operator before its resources. Custom resources often carry a finalizer, a marker that blocks deletion until a controller finishes cleanup. With the controller gone, nothing clears the marker, and `kubectl delete` hangs with the object stuck in `Terminating`. Delete custom resources first, then uninstall the Operator. Removing a finalizer by hand skips that cleanup and can leave external resources behind.
quotes: This custom resource has been stuck in Terminating since yesterday.
Its finalizer is waiting for the Kubernetes Operator, and someone uninstalled it first. Reinstall it so that it can finish the cleanup.

nodes.name: Service mesh
nodes.description: An infrastructure layer of proxies that handles encryption, retries, routing, and metrics for traffic between services.
nodes.markdown:
A service mesh is an infrastructure layer that handles network communication between services using proxies, so applications do not each implement that logic. Traffic passes through a proxy on the way in and out, and a central component configures all the proxies. Istio and Linkerd are examples.

| Feature         | What the mesh does                                           |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Mutual TLS      | Encrypts traffic and verifies both sides' identities         |
| Traffic routing | Splits by weight, for example for a [canary release](node:Canary%20release) |
| Reliability     | Applies retries, timeouts, and circuit breaking (cutting off a failing dependency) |
| Telemetry       | Reports request rate, errors, and latency per service        |

A mesh has a data plane, the proxies that carry traffic, and its own control component, separate from the [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes) [control plane](node:Control%20plane). The traditional data plane injects a sidecar proxy [container](node:Container) into each [Pod](node:Pod). Newer designs, such as Istio's ambient mode, move much of the work to shared per-node proxies.

A mesh adds a hop to every call, proxy memory and CPU, and another system to upgrade and debug. Adopt one for a specific need, such as required encryption between many services. A few services can often manage with a library and a plain [Service](node:Kubernetes%20Service).

Sidecars have known startup and shutdown problems. An application that makes a network call before its proxy is ready fails at boot, which can look random. A Job (a workload that runs to completion) can hang because its main container finished while the sidecar kept running. Kubernetes native sidecars, declared as init containers with `restartPolicy: Always`, address both.

Retries also need coordination. If three layers each try a request three times, one failing call can become 27 attempts against a service that is already struggling.
quotes: The app fails its first DB call on boot, but only since we added the service mesh.
The sidecar isn't ready when your app starts. Switch to native sidecars so the proxy comes up first.

nodes.name: Infrastructure as code
nodes.description: Defining servers, networks, and other infrastructure in version-controlled files that tools apply automatically.
nodes.markdown:
Infrastructure as code (IaC) is the practice of defining servers, networks, databases, and permissions in version-controlled files, then using a tool to create and update them. The files replace manual work in a cloud console. A change to infrastructure becomes a commit that can be reviewed, tested, and reverted.

It addresses a familiar situation: production was built by hand over several years, nobody knows why one firewall rule exists, and staging differs in ways no one can list. When someone has to rebuild after a failure, the only documentation is the running system. With IaC, the definition is written down and can be run again.

IaC tools take one of two approaches:

| Approach    | You write                  | Tool's job                              | Examples                        |
| ----------- | -------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| Declarative | The desired end state      | Work out the changes needed             | [Terraform](node:Terraform), CloudFormation |
| Imperative  | The steps to perform       | Run those steps in order                | Shell scripts, cloud SDK calls  |

Declarative tools are the usual choice because the same file can be applied repeatedly. If the infrastructure already matches, nothing happens. An imperative script that creates a server will often create a second one when it runs again, unless it is written to check first.

A typical workflow puts changes through a [pipeline](node:Pipeline): open a pull request, generate a preview of what will change, have someone review that preview, and apply after merging. The preview matters, because a small edit can have a large effect, such as replacing a database. [Policy as code](node:Policy%20as%20code) can check the preview automatically.

IaC only works while the code stays authoritative. Emergency edits in the console create [configuration drift](node:Configuration%20drift), and the next apply may silently undo them. Credentials should also stay out of these files and come from [secrets management](node:Secrets%20management).
quotes: How long would it take to recreate the staging VPC if someone deleted it?
Days, since it was all clicked together. We should bring it under infrastructure as code before we need to find out.

nodes.name: Terraform
nodes.description: A declarative infrastructure as code tool that compares configuration with recorded state and applies the difference.
nodes.markdown:
Terraform is a declarative [infrastructure as code](node:Infrastructure%20as%20code) tool from HashiCorp. You describe resources in HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language), and Terraform works out what to create, change, or delete to reach that description. Plugins called providers connect it to AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, Cloudflare, and many other APIs. OpenTofu is an open-source fork with a largely compatible workflow.

```hcl
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "logs" {
  bucket = "acme-app-logs"

  lifecycle {
    prevent_destroy = true
  }
}
```

| Command             | What it does                                                  |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `terraform init`    | Downloads providers and connects to the state backend         |
| `terraform plan`    | Shows the changes it would make, without making them          |
| `terraform apply`   | Makes the changes after confirmation                          |
| `terraform destroy` | Deletes everything the configuration manages                  |

To build a plan, Terraform compares three things: your configuration, its record of what it manages in [Terraform state](node:Terraform%20state), and the real resources as reported by the provider. Differences found in the real resources are [configuration drift](node:Configuration%20drift).

A plan can propose destroying a database after a small edit. Some attributes cannot be changed on an existing resource, so changing one means deleting and recreating it. The plan marks this as `-/+` with `# forces replacement` beside the attribute. Renaming a resource block has a similar effect, because Terraform sees one resource removed and another added. A `moved` block tells it that the two are the same.

Read every plan before applying, especially lines containing `destroy` or `replace`. Apply the saved plan with `terraform plan -out=tfplan` followed by `terraform apply tfplan`, so that what was reviewed is what runs. Use `prevent_destroy` on resources that hold data. It makes any plan that would destroy the resource fail, although removing the block from the configuration removes that protection.
quotes: Terraform wants to replace the production database. I only changed one setting.
That setting forces replacement. Stop before applying, and find a way to migrate it without recreating the instance.

nodes.name: Terraform state
nodes.description: The file where Terraform records which real resources it manages, mapping configuration to actual infrastructure IDs.
nodes.markdown:
[Terraform](node:Terraform) state is the data file in which Terraform records the real resources it manages. It maps each block in your configuration, such as `aws_instance.web`, to an actual ID in the provider, such as `i-0abc123`, along with the attributes last seen. Without this mapping, Terraform has no way to know that a server in your account belongs to a given block.

By default state is a local file called `terraform.tfstate`. Teams store it in a remote backend so that everyone works from the same copy:

```hcl
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket       = "acme-terraform-state"
    key          = "prod/network.tfstate"
    region       = "eu-west-1"
    encrypt      = true
    use_lockfile = true
  }
}
```

Most state incidents fall into a few patterns:

| Problem                  | What you see                                    | Response                                   |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| State lost               | Plan wants to create everything again           | Restore a backup, or import resources      |
| Concurrent applies       | State lock error, or corruption if no locking   | Use locking, and run applies in a [pipeline](node:Pipeline) |
| Stale lock               | `Error acquiring the state lock` after a crash  | Confirm nothing is running, then `force-unlock` |
| Resource renamed         | Plan shows destroy and create                   | Add a `moved` block                        |
| Resource created by hand | Terraform ignores it                            | Bring it in with an `import` block         |

State often holds secrets. Database passwords and generated keys are stored in it in plain text, even when marked `sensitive` in the configuration, which only hides them from command output. Never commit it to Git. Keep it in an encrypted backend with restricted access, and treat read access to state as access to those credentials.

Enable versioning on the storage bucket, so that a damaged state file can be restored. Avoid hand-editing the file, and use `terraform state` subcommands when you need to change it. Splitting large projects into several smaller states also reduces the impact of a mistake and keeps plans fast.
quotes: Terraform says it needs to create all 140 resources, but they already exist.
It's reading empty Terraform state. Check that the backend key is right before anyone applies anything.

nodes.name: Configuration drift
nodes.description: The gap that opens when live infrastructure no longer matches its declared configuration, often after manual changes.
nodes.markdown:
Configuration drift is the difference that develops between what your configuration declares and what is actually running. It usually starts with a reasonable action: during an incident, someone opens a port in the cloud console, edits a [Kubernetes Deployment](node:Kubernetes%20Deployment) with `kubectl edit`, or changes a setting on one server over SSH. The fix works, and nobody updates the code.

Drift has two recognisable consequences. The first is a hotfix that disappears. Weeks later, someone runs a routine [Terraform](node:Terraform) apply, the tool restores the declared value, and the incident returns. The second is environments that behave differently for reasons no one can find, where a bug appears in production and cannot be reproduced in staging because their settings are no longer alike.

Detection depends on the layer:

| Layer          | How to detect drift                                                     |
| -------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Cloud resources | A scheduled `terraform plan`, alerting on any non-empty result         |
| [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes) | A [GitOps](node:GitOps) controller reporting an out-of-sync state       |
| Servers        | A [configuration management](node:Configuration%20management) run in check mode |

Once found, each difference needs a decision:

| Decision | When                                     | Action                                  |
| -------- | ---------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Adopt    | The live change is correct               | Update the code to match                |
| Revert   | The live change was a mistake            | Apply the code                          |
| Ignore   | Something else legitimately manages it   | Exclude the field, such as with `ignore_changes` |

Some differences are expected. A [Horizontal Pod Autoscaler](node:Horizontal%20Pod%20Autoscaler) changes replica counts by design, so the replica field should not be owned by the manifest as well.

To prevent drift, restrict write access to production, keep a fast emergency route through the normal [pipeline](node:Pipeline), and require a follow-up commit after any manual fix. [Immutable infrastructure](node:Immutable%20infrastructure) reduces drift on servers because they are replaced instead of edited.
quotes: The rate limit we raised during Friday's incident is back to the old value.
That was a console change, so it was configuration drift. Today's apply reverted it. Put the new value in the Terraform code.

nodes.name: Immutable infrastructure
nodes.description: An approach where servers and containers are never changed in place. Each change builds a new version and replaces the old.
nodes.markdown:
Immutable infrastructure is an approach in which running servers and [containers](node:Container) are never modified after they are deployed. To change anything, whether an application version, a package, or a setting, you build a new image and replace the old instances with it. The image can be a [container image](node:Container%20image) or a virtual machine image built with a tool such as Packer.

| Aspect          | Mutable                           | Immutable                         |
| --------------- | --------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Applying a change | Update the running server       | Build a new image and replace it  |
| Server history  | Accumulates over its lifetime     | Exactly what the image contains   |
| Failed update   | Can leave a partial state         | New instance fails, old one remains |
| Going back      | Reverse each change               | Redeploy the previous image       |

The approach addresses the "snowflake server", a machine that has been patched and adjusted by hand for years until nobody can recreate it, and everyone avoids rebooting it. Replacing instances routinely prevents that history from forming and removes most [configuration drift](node:Configuration%20drift) on the host.

Immutability has requirements. Anything that must survive replacement, such as uploaded files, databases, and logs, has to live outside the instance in external storage or a logging service. Build and deployment must be automated, because a small change now means a full build and rollout. Configuration that varies by environment is supplied at startup, so that one [build artifact](node:Build%20artifact) works everywhere.

Debugging habits also change. A fix patched onto a live server vanishes at the next deployment or scaling event, so it has to go into the image definition. A [rollback](node:Rollback) means redeploying the previous image, provided data changes remain compatible. [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes) works this way by default: changing a [Pod](node:Pod) template creates new Pods and removes the old ones.
quotes: I patched the config on that box last week. Why has the bug come back?
We run immutable infrastructure, so autoscaling replaced that instance. The fix needs to go in the image build.

nodes.name: GitOps
nodes.description: Operating systems from declarative config in Git, with an agent that continuously pulls it and reconciles the live state.
nodes.markdown:
GitOps is an operating model in which a Git repository holds the declared state of a system, and an automated agent continuously makes the live system match it. To change production, you merge a commit. Git supplies the review, audit history, and a way to revert, while the agent does the applying. Argo CD and Flux are common agents for [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes).

The model differs from a traditional deployment [pipeline](node:Pipeline) in the direction of access:

| Aspect          | Push-based [CI](node:Continuous%20integration)/CD                     | Pull-based GitOps                       |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------- |
| Who applies     | The CI job                           | An agent inside the cluster             |
| Credentials     | CI holds cluster access              | Cluster holds read access to Git        |
| When it runs    | Once, on a pipeline trigger          | Continuously                            |
| Manual changes  | Remain until the next deploy         | Detected, and optionally reverted       |

A typical flow has CI build and publish a [container image](node:Container%20image), then update the image tag in a separate configuration repository. The agent sees the commit and rolls out the change. A [rollback](node:Rollback) is usually a `git revert` of that commit.

Continuous reconciliation can revert manual changes. During an incident, someone runs `kubectl scale` or `kubectl edit`, sees the change take effect, and a minute later it is gone. With self-healing enabled, the agent treats the manual edit as [configuration drift](node:Configuration%20drift) and restores the Git version. To make an emergency change stick, commit it, or explicitly suspend syncing for that application and resume it afterwards.

Plain secrets cannot be stored in Git, so teams commit encrypted values or references to an external store through [secrets management](node:Secrets%20management). Fields changed by controllers, such as replica counts under a [Horizontal Pod Autoscaler](node:Horizontal%20Pod%20Autoscaler), must be excluded or they will fight the agent.
quotes: I scaled the API to ten replicas and it dropped back to four by itself.
Argo reverted it. We use GitOps, so the repo wins. Open a PR changing the replica count.

nodes.name: Configuration management
nodes.description: Using tools to install software and keep settings consistent on existing servers, such as with Ansible, Puppet, or Chef.
nodes.markdown:
Configuration management is the use of tools to install software, write config files, manage users, and keep services running on existing servers in a defined way. Instead of logging in to each machine, you describe the desired setup once and apply it across a fleet. Ansible, Puppet, Chef, and Salt are established examples.

```yaml
- name: Ensure nginx is installed
  ansible.builtin.apt:
    name: nginx
    state: present

- name: Ensure nginx is running
  ansible.builtin.service:
    name: nginx
    state: started
    enabled: true
```

The important property is idempotence: running the same configuration many times gives the same result as running it once. The task above installs nginx only when it is missing. Compare a shell script containing `echo "option" >> app.conf`, which appends a duplicate line on every run until the service refuses to start or behaves strangely.

Tools differ in how changes reach a machine:

| Model | How it works                                 | Examples      | Trade-off                                  |
| ----- | -------------------------------------------- | ------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Push  | A control machine connects, often over SSH   | Ansible       | No agent, but runs only when triggered     |
| Pull  | An agent on each server fetches its config   | Puppet, Chef  | Corrects drift regularly, but needs agents |

Configuration management is often confused with [infrastructure as code](node:Infrastructure%20as%20code) tools for provisioning. [Terraform](node:Terraform) typically creates the server, network, and disk, and configuration management sets up what runs inside the machine. The two are commonly used together.

These tools only manage what they are told to manage. A package installed by hand stays on the machine even after the playbook is corrected, so long-lived servers still gather [configuration drift](node:Configuration%20drift). A run can also fail halfway through a fleet, leaving some hosts updated and others not.

[Container](node:Container)-based systems reduce the need for this work, because the software is baked into an [image](node:Container%20image) and replaced under [immutable infrastructure](node:Immutable%20infrastructure). Configuration management remains useful for virtual machines, network devices, and building base images.
quotes: Half the fleet has the new TLS settings and the other half doesn't.
The Ansible run stopped at host 40. It's idempotent, so fix the failure and run the configuration management playbook again.

nodes.name: Policy as code
nodes.description: Writing security and compliance rules as executable code that automatically checks and blocks infrastructure changes.
nodes.markdown:
Policy as code is the practice of writing organisational rules as machine-readable code, so that tools can evaluate changes against them automatically. Rules such as "no public storage buckets", "[containers](node:Container) must not run as root", or "[images](node:Container%20image) must come from our registry" are versioned, reviewed, and tested in the same way as application code. Open Policy Agent (with its Rego language), Kyverno, and HashiCorp Sentinel are examples.

Written guidelines depend on someone remembering them during review. A policy engine gives the same answer every time and reports which rule failed.

The same rule can be enforced at several points:

| Enforcement point         | What is checked                         | Effect of a violation            |
| ------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| Developer machine or PR   | Manifests and config files              | Early feedback                   |
| [Pipeline](node:Pipeline) | A [Terraform](node:Terraform) plan or built image | Blocks the merge or deploy |
| [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes) admission | Objects sent to the API server          | The API request is rejected      |
| Runtime audit             | Resources that already exist            | Reports or remediates            |

Earlier checks give faster feedback, while admission control is harder to bypass. An admission controller is a [control plane](node:Control%20plane) plugin that can inspect or modify a request before it is stored. Policy engines usually attach as admission webhooks, so a blocked deploy appears as an error such as `admission webhook "..." denied the request`.

A new rule in blocking mode can break existing deployments. Run it in audit mode first, fix or exempt what it would reject, then enforce it. Each policy should tell the developer how to comply.

Admission webhooks also add an availability risk. If a webhook is set to `failurePolicy: Fail` and its service goes down, every matching API request is refused, which can block new [Pods](node:Pod), including the replacement for the webhook itself. Run it with multiple replicas, and exclude system namespaces.
quotes: My deploy just got rejected by an admission webhook.
That's policy as code. The rule says containers can't run as root, so set `runAsNonRoot` and apply it again.

nodes.name: Secrets management
nodes.description: Storing, distributing, rotating, and auditing credentials such as passwords, API keys, and certificates.
nodes.markdown:
Secrets management is the practice of controlling credentials such as passwords, API keys, tokens, and certificates throughout their lifecycle. It covers storage, access, delivery to applications, rotation (replacing them with new values), and auditing. HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, and Google Secret Manager are examples of dedicated stores.

The typical failure is a credential committed to Git. Deleting it in a later commit does not help, because it remains in the repository's history and in every clone. Once a secret has been pushed, treat it as compromised: revoke it, issue a new one, and check the access logs. Secret scanners in pre-commit hooks and [pipelines](node:Pipeline) can catch many of these before they land.

Approaches form a ladder:

| Level | Approach                     | Remaining weakness                          |
| ----- | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| 1     | Hardcoded in source          | Visible to anyone with the code             |
| 2     | `.env` files on servers      | Copied around, rarely rotated               |
| 3     | [CI](node:Continuous%20integration) or platform secret store | Long-lived, limited audit                   |
| 4     | [Kubernetes Secret](node:Kubernetes%20Secret), encrypted at rest | Readable by anyone who can create [Pods](node:Pod) in the namespace |
| 5     | Central secrets manager      | Applications still hold static values       |
| 6     | Short-lived dynamic credentials | Depends on the issuer being available    |

Dynamic credentials are issued on demand and expire automatically, so a leaked value has a short useful life. With workload identity or OIDC federation (trading a signed identity token for temporary access), a CI job or Pod receives temporary cloud permissions without a stored credential.

Rotation fails when nobody knows which services use a key, so the first attempt causes an outage. Automate it, and support two valid credentials during the changeover.

Secrets also leak through less obvious channels: logs, error reports, [Terraform state](node:Terraform%20state), and [image layers](node:Image%20layer). Inject values at runtime, and keep them out of builds and output.
quotes: I removed the leaked AWS key in the next commit, so we're fine, right?
No, it's still in history. Revoke it now. Then move it into secrets management.

nodes.name: Rolling deployment
nodes.description: A release strategy that replaces instances in small batches, so the service stays available while two versions run together.
nodes.markdown:
A rolling deployment is a release strategy that replaces running instances of an application with a new version in small batches. Capacity stays mostly available throughout, and no second full environment is needed. It is the default update strategy for a [Kubernetes Deployment](node:Kubernetes%20Deployment).

[Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes) controls the pace with two settings. `maxSurge` is how many extra [Pods](node:Pod) may exist above the desired count, and `maxUnavailable` is how many may be missing. With 4 replicas, `maxSurge: 1`, and `maxUnavailable: 0`:

| Step | Old Pods | New Pods | What happens                         |
| ---- | -------- | -------- | ------------------------------------ |
| 1    | 4        | 1        | One new Pod starts                   |
| 2    | 3        | 1        | It becomes ready, one old Pod leaves |
| 3    | 3        | 2        | Next new Pod starts                  |
| 4    | 2        | 2        | It becomes ready, one old Pod leaves |
| 5    | 0        | 4        | The pattern repeats until complete   |

Two versions serve traffic at the same time during the rollout, which causes intermittent errors that appear only during deploys. A page from the new version calls an API endpoint, the call lands on an old Pod that lacks it, and the request fails until a refresh. Each release must stay compatible with the one before it, which is the purpose of [expand and contract](node:Expand%20and%20contract).

Two details prevent dropped requests. A [readiness probe](node:Readiness%20probe) keeps traffic away from a new Pod until it can serve. Graceful shutdown lets an old Pod finish in-flight requests after `SIGTERM`, before the grace period (30 seconds by default) ends in `SIGKILL`.

A [rollback](node:Rollback) is another rolling update in the opposite direction, so it takes time. For an instant switch, use a [blue-green deployment](node:Blue-green%20deployment). To measure impact on a small share of traffic first, use a [canary release](node:Canary%20release).
quotes: We get a handful of 404s from the API on every deploy, then they stop.
During the rolling deployment, new frontends hit old backends. Ship the endpoint first, then the frontend that calls it.

nodes.name: Blue-green deployment
nodes.description: A release strategy that runs two full environments and switches all traffic from the old version to the new at once.
nodes.markdown:
A blue-green deployment is a release strategy that keeps two production environments and moves traffic between them in one switch. "Blue" runs the current version and receives all traffic. "Green" gets the new version and is tested while idle. When it looks correct, a router or load balancer (a component that spreads traffic across servers) points everyone at green.

| Step | Blue            | Green           | What happens                           |
| ---- | --------------- | --------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| 1    | Live            | Idle            | Deploy the new version to green        |
| 2    | Live            | Under test      | Run smoke tests against green directly |
| 3    | Idle            | Live            | Switch traffic to green                |
| 4    | Idle, on standby | Live           | Watch metrics, keep blue running       |
| 5    | Next target     | Live            | Blue becomes the next release target   |

The main benefit is a fast [rollback](node:Rollback): if green misbehaves, the router points back at blue, with no rebuild or redeploy. Unlike a [rolling deployment](node:Rolling%20deployment), users do not see a long period with two versions mixed. In [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes), one simple form runs two [Deployments](node:Kubernetes%20Deployment) and changes the label selector on a [Service](node:Kubernetes%20Service).

Both environments typically share one database, which limits rollback. If green's release drops or renames a column, switching back to blue fails. Schema changes need to work with both versions, using [expand and contract](node:Expand%20and%20contract).

The switch also has side effects:

- Green starts with cold caches, so latency can jump after the cutover.
- Existing long-lived connections, such as WebSockets, may stay on blue until they are closed.
- DNS-based switching is slow and uneven, because clients cache old answers.
- Background workers in both environments may process the same jobs unless one is paused.

Running two full environments can double compute cost, so many teams create green on demand and remove it afterwards.
quotes: Green's error rate just doubled after the cutover.
Flip the load balancer back to blue. That's why we keep it running after a blue-green deployment.

nodes.name: Canary release
nodes.description: A release strategy that sends a small share of real traffic to a new version and widens it only if metrics stay healthy.
nodes.markdown:
A canary release is a release strategy that sends a small share of real production traffic to a new version, compares its behaviour with the current version, and increases the share only if it stays healthy. If it degrades, traffic returns to the old version, so the failure affects a small group of users.

A typical progression looks like this, though the percentages and timings vary:

| Stage | Traffic to new version | Hold       | Promote if                         |
| ----- | ---------------------- | ---------- | ---------------------------------- |
| 1     | 1%                     | 10 minutes | Errors and latency match baseline  |
| 2     | 10%                    | 30 minutes | Same, plus key business metrics    |
| 3     | 50%                    | 30 minutes | Same                               |
| 4     | 100%                   | Done       | Old version removed                |

A canary catches problems that tests miss, because real traffic has data, clients, and load patterns that staging lacks. It only helps if someone defines what "healthy" means before the release. Compare the canary with a baseline running the old version at the same moment, because comparing against yesterday's numbers mixes in normal traffic changes. Tools such as Argo Rollouts and Flagger can automate promotion and [rollback](node:Rollback) based on these metrics.

Traffic splitting needs some care. A plain [Kubernetes Service](node:Kubernetes%20Service) spreads connections across [Pods](node:Pod), so a percentage can only be approximated by the replica ratio, such as one canary in ten Pods. Exact weights need an [Ingress](node:Ingress) controller or [service mesh](node:Service%20mesh) that supports them.

Small canaries have blind spots. At 1% on a quiet service, there may be too few requests for a problem to show up, and slow failures such as memory leaks can outlast the hold time. Assign users consistently, so that one person does not bounce between versions. As in a [rolling deployment](node:Rolling%20deployment), both versions must work with the same database.
quotes: Should we ship the new ranking model to everyone tonight?
Do a canary release at 5% first and compare error rate and checkout conversion against the baseline for an hour.

nodes.name: Dark launch
nodes.description: Running new code in production against real traffic or data, while users continue to see only the existing behaviour.
nodes.markdown:
A dark launch is the release of new code to production so that it runs against real traffic or data while users continue to see the existing behaviour. The new path does its work, but its output is discarded or logged for comparison. This tests performance and correctness under production conditions before anyone depends on the result.

A common form is shadow traffic. The service handles each request as usual and also sends a copy to the new implementation asynchronously. The user receives the old response, while engineers compare the two responses and watch the new system's latency and error rate. A [feature flag](node:Feature%20flag) often controls which requests are mirrored, and a [service mesh](node:Service%20mesh) can mirror them at the network level.

Dark launches are often confused with neighbouring strategies:

| Strategy                                | Runs in production? | Do users see the result? |
| --------------------------------------- | ------------------- | ------------------------ |
| Dark launch                             | Yes                 | No                       |
| [Canary release](node:Canary%20release) | Yes                 | A small share of users   |
| Feature flag rollout                    | Yes                 | Chosen users             |

The technique suits risky backend replacements, such as a rewritten pricing engine or a new search index, because staging rarely reproduces real data shapes and volume.

Side effects are the main hazard. If a mirrored request sends an email, charges a card, or writes to a shared database, it happens twice, and customers see duplicates from a feature meant to be invisible. Stub out writes and external calls in the dark path, or point them at isolated storage.

Dark traffic is also real load, and extra calls to a shared dependency can slow the live path. Sample a small percentage first, send copies with strict timeouts, and keep a way to turn mirroring off. Remove the comparison code after launch.
quotes: How do we know the new pricing engine handles real orders?
Dark launch it. Mirror 10% of requests, discard its output, and diff its prices against the old engine for a week.

nodes.name: Rollback
nodes.description: Returning a system to a previous known-good version after a bad release. It restores code, but not necessarily data.
nodes.markdown:
A rollback is the act of returning a system to a previous known-good version after a release causes problems. It is usually a quick way to restore service, because it reuses something that has already run in production.

The available method depends on how the release was made:

| Method                  | How it works                                                    | Typical speed |
| ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------- |
| [Feature flag](node:Feature%20flag) off | Disables the code path with no deploy           | Seconds       |
| Traffic switch          | Points back at the old [blue-green](node:Blue-green%20deployment) environment | Seconds to minutes |
| Abort a [canary](node:Canary%20release) | Returns the traffic share to the old version    | Seconds to minutes |
| Redeploy old artifact   | Rolls out the previous [build artifact](node:Build%20artifact)  | Minutes       |
| `kubectl rollout undo`  | Restores the previous [Deployment](node:Kubernetes%20Deployment) revision | Minutes |
| `git revert` with [GitOps](node:GitOps) | Reverts the commit and lets the agent sync | Minutes       |

A rollback sometimes fails to fix the incident. The old code is running again and errors continue, because the release changed something other than code. Common causes:

- A database migration dropped or rewrote a column that the old version needs.
- New code already wrote data in a format the old code cannot read.
- A [ConfigMap](node:ConfigMap), [Secret](node:Kubernetes%20Secret), or infrastructure change is not versioned with the release.
- The real cause was never the release, such as a failing dependency or a traffic spike.
- The previous artifact was deleted by a retention policy.

Plan for this before release: keep schema changes backward compatible using [expand and contract](node:Expand%20and%20contract), retain recent artifacts, and rehearse the procedure.

Rolling forward, meaning shipping a fix as a new version, can be safer when the fix is small and understood, or when data has changed so that old code cannot run.
quotes: We rolled back twenty minutes ago and checkout is still failing.
Then it isn't only the code. That release ran a migration, so the rollback put old code on the new schema.

nodes.name: Expand and contract
nodes.description: A way to make breaking schema or API changes in compatible steps, adding the new form before removing the old.
nodes.markdown:
Expand and contract, also called parallel change, is a way to make a breaking change to a database schema or API through a series of compatible steps. You first add the new form alongside the old one, move everything across, and remove the old form only when nothing uses it. Old and new application versions keep working at every step.

The technique exists because deployments are not instantaneous. During a [rolling deployment](node:Rolling%20deployment), old and new code run at the same time against one database. If a release renames `name` to `full_name` in a single migration, every old instance starts failing with "column does not exist" the moment the migration runs. Reversing the application with a [rollback](node:Rollback) does not help, because the old code needs a column that is gone.

Renaming that column safely takes several releases:

| Step | Phase    | Change                                         | Safe to roll back? |
| ---- | -------- | ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------ |
| 1    | Expand   | Add nullable `full_name` column                | Yes                |
| 2    | Migrate  | Deploy code that writes to both columns        | Yes                |
| 3    | Migrate  | Backfill existing rows in small batches        | Yes                |
| 4    | Migrate  | Deploy code that reads from `full_name`        | Yes, still dual-writing |
| 5    | Migrate  | Deploy code that writes only `full_name`       | To step 4. Earlier needs a re-sync |
| 6    | Contract | Drop `name` after confirming nothing uses it   | No                 |

Step 6 is the only destructive change and can wait until the team is confident. Verify the backfill first, and check for other readers such as reports and scheduled jobs.

The same pattern applies to APIs: add the new field, migrate clients, then remove the old one. [Continuous deployment](node:Continuous%20deployment) depends on this pattern, at the cost of more releases and temporary dual-write code.
quotes: Can I rename this column in today's migration?
Not in one step, because the old [pods](node:Pod) will crash mid-deploy. Use expand and contract: add the new column first and drop the old one next week.

nodes.name: Software supply chain
nodes.description: Everything that goes into building and shipping software, including dependencies, tools, pipelines, images, and registries.
nodes.markdown:
The software supply chain is everything involved in producing and delivering a piece of software: source code, third-party dependencies, base [images](node:Container%20image), compilers, [pipelines](node:Pipeline), registries, and deployment tools. Your application inherits the trust of each link. Installing one package can pull in many others that nobody on the team chose directly.

A supply chain attack compromises one of those links instead of the application. The malicious code then arrives through a normal, trusted update, with no vulnerability in your own code:

| Attack              | How it works                                                        | Defence                                    |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Typosquatting       | Publishes a package with a name close to a popular one              | Review new dependencies                    |
| Dependency confusion | Public package shadows an internal name                            | Scoped names, a controlled [artifact registry](node:Artifact%20registry) |
| Maintainer takeover | A trusted package gets a malicious release                          | [Dependency pinning](node:Dependency%20pinning), delayed updates |
| Install scripts     | Package runs code during installation                               | Disable scripts where possible             |
| [CI](node:Continuous%20integration) compromise | Attacker steals pipeline secrets or alters the build                | Least privilege, pinned CI actions         |
| Tampered artifact   | Image or package is altered after the build                         | Signing and digest verification            |

Defences work in layers. Know what you ship, using an [SBOM](node:SBOM). Find known flaws with [image scanning](node:Image%20scanning) and dependency audits. Control what enters the build with pinned versions and a proxy registry. Prove where artifacts came from through signing, with a tool such as Sigstore's cosign, and through provenance, which is a signed record of how and from what an artifact was built. The SLSA framework (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) defines progressive levels for build integrity.

A signature has no effect unless something checks it, so verify it at deploy time, for example with [policy as code](node:Policy%20as%20code) in a [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes) admission controller.
quotes: Why does the build need network access to run a postinstall script from some transitive package?
It doesn't, and that's a software supply chain risk. Disable install scripts in CI and allowlist the few that need them.

nodes.name: Dependency pinning
nodes.description: Fixing dependencies to exact versions or hashes so that every build uses the same inputs and updates happen deliberately.
nodes.markdown:
Dependency pinning is the practice of fixing each dependency to an exact version or content hash, so that a build uses the same inputs every time. Without it, a version range or moving tag can resolve to something new between two builds.

The familiar symptom is a build that passed on Friday and fails on Monday with no commits in between. A package several levels down published a new release, the range accepted it, and CI picked it up. [Semantic versioning](node:Semantic%20versioning) ranges rely on maintainers classifying each change correctly, and on nobody publishing a malicious update.

Pinning has several levels of strength:

| Level          | Example                         | What it guarantees                      |
| -------------- | ------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Range          | `"express": "^4.18.0"`          | Compatible versions, by convention      |
| Exact version  | `"express": "4.18.2"`           | That package only, not its dependencies |
| Lockfile       | `package-lock.json`, `poetry.lock` | The full dependency tree              |
| Content hash   | `integrity: sha512-...`         | The exact bytes                         |

Commit the lockfile and install from it in CI. `npm ci`, for example, installs precisely what the lockfile says and fails if it disagrees with `package.json`, while `npm install` may update it.

The same rule applies beyond language packages. A [container image](node:Container%20image) tag can be moved, so pin a base image by digest. Pin CI actions to a full commit SHA, because a tag such as `v4` can be repointed:

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-slim@sha256:<digest>
```

```yaml
- uses: actions/checkout@<full-commit-sha> # v4
```

Pinning protects the [software supply chain](node:Software%20supply%20chain) from unexpected changes, but it also stops security fixes arriving automatically. Tools such as Renovate and Dependabot address this by opening regular pull requests that bump versions and run through [continuous integration](node:Continuous%20integration). A short delay before adopting new releases gives others time to spot a bad one.
quotes: Nobody touched the repo over the weekend, but the build is red.
The [Dockerfile](node:Dockerfile) runs `npm install` with no lockfile, so a transitive package moved. Add dependency pinning and switch to `npm ci`.

nodes.name: SBOM
nodes.description: A software bill of materials, a machine-readable inventory of the components and versions inside a piece of software.
nodes.markdown:
An SBOM (software bill of materials) is a machine-readable inventory of the components inside a piece of software. For each package it typically records the name, version, supplier, license, a unique identifier, and how components depend on each other. It works like an ingredient list for a [build artifact](node:Build%20artifact) or [container image](node:Container%20image).

The practical case for one appears when a serious vulnerability is announced in a widely used library. The immediate question is "are we affected, and where?". Without an inventory, engineers search repositories by hand and still miss copies pulled in several levels down or bundled inside a vendor's image. With SBOMs stored for every release, the answer is a query across existing data.

Two standard formats are in common use:

| Format    | Maintained by | Origin and emphasis                       |
| --------- | ------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| SPDX      | Linux Foundation | Began with license compliance          |
| CycloneDX | OWASP         | Began with application security           |

Tools such as Syft and Trivy can generate either format. Generate the SBOM in the [pipeline](node:Pipeline) at build time, from the final artifact when possible, because a source repository does not show what the base image added. Store it with the artifact and sign it, so that it can be tied to one specific build as part of the [software supply chain](node:Software%20supply%20chain).

An SBOM says a component is present, without saying whether the vulnerable function is ever called. A companion format, VEX (Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange), lets a supplier state whether a product is affected by a given flaw. Generators can also miss statically linked libraries, copied source files, and binaries downloaded during a build.

The list of known vulnerabilities grows after a build, so stored SBOMs should be re-checked regularly, using the same vulnerability data as [image scanning](node:Image%20scanning).
quotes: A critical CVE just dropped in that XML library. Do we ship it anywhere?
Query the SBOMs for every production release. That'll list the affected services without us grepping all the repos.

nodes.name: Image scanning
nodes.description: Automatically checking a container image's packages against databases of known vulnerabilities.
nodes.markdown:
Image scanning is the automated inspection of a [container image](node:Container%20image) to find known security problems. A scanner identifies the operating system packages and application libraries in each [image layer](node:Image%20layer), then compares their versions against vulnerability databases, reporting matches as CVEs (public identifiers for known flaws). Trivy, Grype, and the scanners built into many [container registries](node:Container%20registry) are examples.

Scans can run at several points:

| Where                           | Purpose                                   |
| ------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| Developer machine               | Early feedback before pushing             |
| [Pipeline](node:Pipeline)       | Block a build that fails the threshold    |
| Registry                        | Scan on push, and rescan stored images    |
| [Kubernetes](node:Kubernetes) admission | Reject images without a passing result    |
| Running workloads               | Find newly disclosed issues in production |

Rescanning matters because an image that was clean last month can show a critical finding today, when a flaw is disclosed in a package it already contains.

Teams adopting a scanner usually meet alert fatigue first. The initial report on a full-distribution base image can list hundreds of findings, many with no available fix or in code the application never runs. If the pipeline blocks on all of them, developers learn to bypass it. A workable gate fails only on high or critical findings that have a fix available, with time-limited exceptions for the rest.

To reduce findings, use a slim or distroless base through a [multi-stage build](node:Multi-stage%20build), and rebuild regularly. If the base uses [dependency pinning](node:Dependency%20pinning), update the pin, or the rebuild picks up no fixes.

Linux distributions often backport fixes without changing the upstream version number, which can produce false positives in tools that ignore distribution advisories. A clean scan covers only known issues in detected components. It does not find flaws in your own code or zero-day vulnerabilities (flaws not yet public).
quotes: The scanner reports 312 CVEs and [CI](node:Continuous%20integration) is blocked.
Most are in the full Debian base. Move to a slim image, then have image scanning fail only on fixable criticals.
